docs.title: Kajar
docs.text:
Chrono Trigger

A byte-exact decompilation of the 1995 classic, one matched routine at a time

But… the future refused to change.

Game Over screen 170,895code bytes matched47.69%of all game code10,748data bytes matched2,403functions matched2,403functions readable2,403functions verified358,356bytes of 65C816 code 2026-08-06: 10,013 bytes matched, 60 matched2026-08-07: 12,583 bytes matched, 76 matched2026-08-09: 13,752 bytes matched, 85 matched2026-08-10: 13,914 bytes matched, 86 matched2026-08-11: 16,291 bytes matched, 94 matched2026-08-12: 19,800 bytes matched, 104 matched2026-08-14: 23,885 bytes matched, 164 matched2026-09-19: 25,363 bytes matched, 186 matched2026-09-22: 26,000 bytes matched, 206 matched2026-09-24: 26,828 bytes matched, 207 matched2026-10-08: 128,218 bytes matched, 1,715 matched, 1,715 readable, 1,715 verified2026-10-09: 154,931 code bytes matched, 10,444 data bytes, 2,184 matched, 2,184 readable, 2,184 verified2026-08-06 · 10,013 B2026-10-09 · 154,931 BMatched code bytes by working day, from the code repo's history (days before the code/data split count every matched byte).

Every number above is generated; see Progress.

Welcome to ChronoRET, a byte-exact matching decompilation of Chrono Trigger (SNES, US 1.0).

The goal is hand-labeled 65816 assembly that assembles back to a ROM that is bit-for-bit identical to the original 1995 cartridge. A routine only reaches the main branch once it is matched byte for byte, written to the project's readability standard, and approved by an independent review.

This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Square or Square Enix in any way.

docs.title: Project at a glance
docs.text:
Bank What is matched there $C0 The field engine: game loop, frame wait and NMI handler, location loading, map scrolling, object motion, the event script opcodes, the sprite system, and the reset code, header and vectors at the top of the bank $C1 The battle engine: BattleSys_Main and its turn lists, the enemy behaviour scripts, the PC command runner, action scripts, the battle menu, targeting and status bar $C2 The scene mode (tasks, scripts, sprite list, scene loading) and the text window decoder $FD MainInit, the battle helpers bank $C1 calls with JSL, the field HDMA set-up and the location animation set-up $CC, $CF, $FF Copies of matched code kept in other banks: the 8×8 multiply ($CC), a scaled sine and a four-digit number formatter ($CF), the wave tables ($FF)

How much of each bank is matched, and at which level, is generated on the ROM Map and Progress pages.

docs.title: Matched regions
docs.text:
What is matched, bank by bank, is on the ROM Map, generated from the code repository on every update, so it is never out of date. The figures by level, bank and day are on Progress, and every routine of a system is listed on its page under Systems.

The 4 MB ROM is mostly graphics and music data; only about 358 KB is executable 65816 code.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
A routine goes through these steps before it reaches the main branch:

  1. Draft — make draft ADDR=C1:3714 (tools/draft.py) disassembles the routine from its address, tracking the M/X flags, DP and DB, and writes asar source that already uses every name the project has for its operands. It checks that the draft assembles to the original bytes.
  2. Make it readable — the matcher names what the draft could not (RAM, constants, calls, the routine itself) and writes the header: what the routine is for, its CPU state on entry and exit, and anything a reader would not guess. Unknown meanings stay hedged ("probably", Unk names).
  3. Gate — make gate runs the byte-for-byte diff (make diff), proves that every byte the source claims is really emitted by it (make verify), and runs the readability lint (tools/lint_readability.py). The ; Callers block of each header is generated by tools/callers.py, never written by hand.
  4. Review — someone who did not write the routine checks that its names and comments tell the truth. The verdict is a row in a review round file (symbols/reviews/rNNN.csv) that carries the routine's source hash, so any later edit sends it back for review.

Each level includes the one before: matched → readable → verified. The figures are computed by tools/progress.py from the source and the review log; generated files are not committed, and no number is typed by hand.

docs.title: Engine Architecture
docs.text: A high-level map of the Chrono Trigger SNES engine as recovered from matched code. Everything here comes from byte-exact matched routines and their reviewed headers; where a header only infers a meaning ("probably", "not traced"), so does this page. The Systems pages go into each part in more detail.

docs.title: The banks and how they call each other
docs.text:
The code that is matched so far lives in a handful of banks, each with its own job and its own direct-page layout:

Bank Role Direct page $00 (= top of $C0) Reset, interrupt stubs, ROM header and vectors — $FD MainInit, battle helpers called with JSL, field HDMA and animation set-up $4200/$2100 in MainInit; the caller's elsewhere $C0 The field engine: game loop, NMI, maps, objects, event scripts, sprites $0100 (field page), $1D00 for the map code $C2 The scene mode (Loc_Id $01F0 and up), the menu's entry, thread scheduler and shared helpers, and the text window decoder $0000 ($0200 for the text decoder, $0D00 for the menu's NMI) $C1 The battle engine $0000, with DB = $7E

Other banks enter $C0, $C1 and $C2 only through small fixed vector tables:

  • ReentryVectors at $C0:0000: entry 0 is a warm restart (GameLoop_Main), entries 1–4 are JSL targets that tail into ScrollStepAccum, Field_RefreshHdmaLong, MusicCueDispatch and AudioFadeDispatch (see Engine core).
  • BankC2_Entry0000–000C at $C2:0000 (the scene mode and the text window calls) and BankC2_Entry8000/8002/8004 at $C2:8000 (the menu entry, the joypad reader and a command dispatcher).
  • $C1:0000 and on: the battle entry (JSL $C10000 from the field), the exit vector, and a same-bank service dispatcher at $C1:0045 with a 10-entry table at $C1:0051. The vectors themselves are not matched yet; BankC1_BattleStartVec ($C1:8000) and BankC1_Entry8003 ($C1:8003, the inventory and gold services the field's event scripts use) are.

docs.title: Boot sequence
docs.text:
RESET vector → Reset ($00:FF00)
  SEI / CLC / XCE                 native mode
  JML MainInit                    (soft resets come here too)

MainInit ($FD:C000, 215 bytes)
  1. CPU mode, stack S=$06FF, DB=$00, DP=$4200
  2. CPU I/O registers through DP=$4200
  3. DP=$2100, forced blank
  4. PPU registers through DP=$2100
  5. JML GameLoop ($C0:000E)

GameLoop ($C0:000E) — cold init
  InstallNMI / InstallIRQ         JML NmiHandler / IrqHandler into $7E:0500 / $0504
  DP=$0100, InitHW                interrupts off, forced blank
  ClearRAMDMA ×3                  $7E:0000–04FF, $7E:0700–FFFF, $7F:5080–A0FF
  JSL Audio_DriverInit            sound driver (bank $C7)
  JSL BankC2_Entry8004            bank $C2's command dispatcher, A = BankC2_BootArg
  falls into GameLoop_Main

GameLoop_Main ($C0:005D) is also the warm-restart entry: it runs InitHW, reinstalls the interrupt trampolines and dispatches on Loc_Id:

Loc_Id Goes to $0000–$01EF GameLoop_LoadField: a field location $01F0–$81EF JML BankC2_Entry0000: the bank-$C2 scene mode $81F0–$81FE Sys_HaltWithColor: stops the game on one colour $81FF–$FFFF GameLoop_LoadField

Both tests are CPX then BMI, so they branch on bit 15 of the difference, not on a signed compare; what would set bit 15 of Loc_Id is not traced. The independent review of MainInit noted that GameLoop is probably misnamed, since it starts with an init sequence.

docs.title: The field frame
docs.text:
GameLoop_LoadField ($C0:007D) sets DP=$0100 and loads the location once: Field_InitLoadState (reset the field page), LoadLocation (ten load steps and two bank-$FD vectors), Obj_ResetStates, Scene_PostLoadInit (the objects and their init scripts), TileAnimList_Clear and Scene_SettleFrames (the fade-in). Then it falls into the per-frame loop:

GameLoop_FrameBody ($C0:0097) — never returns
  latch newly pressed buttons
  Field_PauseAndMenuInput     Start pauses; menu button → bank $C2 menu round trip
  Field_SceneChangeTick       fades; warps, bank-$C2 calls, tile animations, battles
  Field_FrameUpdate           D-pad, the leader's collision (probably), layer scroll
  Field_ActionButton          action button: an object or treasure in front of the leader
  JSL Field_Unk1F87           the message window: open, draw the text, wait, close
  Field_EventHookDispatch     one of 16 window-effect hooks
  Field_ServiceUnk54          staff credits lines, map redraw requests
  Field_EndOfFrame            object scripts, HDMA, motion, frame builds, OAM shadow
  Field_WaitFrame             wait for the NMI to finish the frame's uploads
  BRA GameLoop_FrameBody

Field_EndOfFrame ($C0:00BF) is not an interrupt handler: it is the end of the frame's game logic. It runs the object script scheduler (Vblank_Unk59D9, Vblank_ReadScanlineCounters), EngFD_UnkC2C1 (HDMA), FdVec_FFF7, the object pass Vblank_UnkA810 (movement, view culling, animation), Field_ProcessAnimQueue (frame builds while there is time left), and tail-jumps to Oam_BuildShadow, which rebuilds the OAM shadow for the next frame.

docs.title: The NMI handshake
docs.text: Field_WaitFrame ($C0:EC60) increments Nmi_FramePending and spins until it is 0 again. NmiHandler ($C0:EA63, entered through the $7E:0500 trampoline) does the frame's uploads only when Nmi_FramePending is set; on a lag frame it skips straight to the register writes. Usually it runs the common uploads (Pal_UploadCgram, Oam_UploadShadow, VramQ_Flush and the map edge uploads), after any extra upload that was requested (a Field_Unk47 upload, or a staff credits line and the Field_Unk36 upload); a map redraw step (Field_MapRedrawDone) is uploaded instead of them. Every NMI then calls the joypad reader (JSL BankC2_Entry8002), writes the window and colour shadows, HDMAEN and INIDISP, and returns with RTI. See Frame cycle and NMI.

docs.title: Scene changes
docs.text:
Field_SceneChangeTick ($C0:0C76) steps the fades in Field_FadeFlags, then acts on Field_SceneFlags:

Request What happens bit 7 Fade out, then warp: copy Loc_Dest* into Loc_Id/Loc_Entry*, reset the stack and restart through ReentryVectors bit 6 Fade out, save the field (Field_SaveState), call BankC2_Entry8000 with an argument from Field_BankC2Arg, restore and fade in bit 4 Run the tile-animation handler for the map tile's state byte (ModeE6_Handler … ModeFC_Handler) otherwise DefaultHandler

DefaultHandler ($C0:16DC) handles three more requests in order: bit 1 steps one map tile and queues its VRAM addresses; bit 5 redraws map layers (running Field_Unk885A frame after frame first); bit 0 is the battle: unless Scene_Unk024C returns carry it calls JSL EngCall_BattleMain, reinstalls the interrupt handlers and rebuilds the field (Scene_Unk0283).

The five tile-animation handlers share one shape: advance the state byte of each affected map tile in Map_TileProps by one, play Audio_SfxTileAnimA, compute the VRAM word address of each map tile's four 8×8 tiles in the 64×32 BG tilemap (Bg_TilemapIndex64x32) into TileAnim_VramAddrs, set the VRAM queue flag and continue in DefaultHandler. They differ in the block they animate: $E6 a 1×2 column, $EC/$EE a 2×2 block, $FA/$FC a 2-wide, 3-tall block (the second of each pair mirrored).

docs.title: Bank $C2 round trips
docs.text:
The field hands control to bank $C2 in two ways:

  • The menu and the bank-$C2 calls. Field_SaveState copies the field's save block ($7E:0920, $14E0 bytes) to $7F:2000 and records the party's positions; the field then calls BankC2_Entry8000 with an argument (1 from the menu button, "very likely the main menu" in its header; 5 from Field_RunBankC2Mode5, meaning unverified). The menu installs its own interrupt handlers, runs its screens as cooperative threads (Menu_RunThreads) and returns with RTL through Menu_Exit, or restarts the game loop through Menu_ExitToGame (see Menu). Afterwards Field_RestoreState rebuilds the field, and Party_ReinitIfChanged runs the init function of each character object again if the party is no longer the one taken at load.
  • The scene mode. For Loc_Id $01F0–$81EF, GameLoop_Main jumps to BankC2_SceneBoot, which installs its own NMI and runs C2Scene_Main. It leaves the scene by jumping to ReentryVectors (C2Scene_Mode2), which restarts the field's game loop. See Scene engine.

docs.title: The battle
docs.text:
JSL $C10000 (from DefaultHandler, at $C0:18A7) reaches the battle entry, which per BattleSys_PumpFrames' header goes JMP $001B → JML $CF:FB65 (clears battle RAM) → $C1:8000 → BattleSys_Main. BattleSys_Main ($C1:8006) never returns: it sets the battle up, then loops pass after pass over the 13 turn lists until a victory, defeat or other end, and leaves through BattleSys_ExitVec ($C1:0006 → $001F → JML $CF:FBE5). Back on the field, Scene_Unk0283 reads FieldBtl_Result and either rebuilds the location in place from the field/battle hand-off block ($7E:29B0–$2C7B), reloads it, or restarts the game.

Inside bank $C1, the service dispatcher at $C1:0045 is reached only by same-bank JSR. The services matched so far: 1 BattleMenu_EnqueueReadyBattler, 2 BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady, 3 BattleSys_UpkeepTwoFrames, 4 BattleSys_RunAction, 5 BattlePos_Query, 7 BattleTgt_RunAreaQuery, 8 BattleSys_VictoryPose, 9 BattleSys_DefeatPose; service 0 ends in Battle_StartPose, and service 6 is not analysed. See Battle engine.

docs.title: RAM-resident interrupt handlers
docs.text:
The native NMI and IRQ vectors can only point into bank $00, so they land on 4-byte stubs that jump on through trampolines in WRAM:

WRAM Stub Installed by Target $7E:0500 NMI_Stub ($00:FF10) InstallNMI (field), C2Scene_InstallInterrupts (scene mode), Menu_InitSystems (menu) NmiHandler ($C0:EA63), C2Scene_NmiHandler ($C2:015E), Menu_Nmi ($C2:840E) $7E:0504 IRQ_Stub ($00:FF14) InstallIRQ, C2Scene_InstallInterrupts, Menu_InitSystems IrqHandler ($C0:ECCC), C2Scene_IrqHandler ($C2:0345), Menu_Irq ($C2:8472)

The trampolines are not set by MainInit. Sys_HaltWithColor sets both to RTI (at $C0:2E4B), and unmatched code in bank $FD ($FD:EAF4) repoints both into that bank (see !NmiTrampoline in ram_engine.inc).

The menu in bank $C2 has handlers of its own, Menu_Nmi ($C2:840E) and Menu_Irq ($C2:8472, a bare RTI): Menu_InitSystems copies the two JMLs at $C2:8406 (Menu_InterruptVectors) over the trampolines. See Frame cycle and NMI.

docs.title: Key field structures
docs.text:
• The field direct page ($0100–$01FF, DP=$0100): Loc_Id at $0100, the frame handshake Nmi_FramePending ($52), the current object Obj_Cur ($6D), the OAM range pointers ($7B–$8B, $DB–$DF) and the fade and scene flags.
  • Per-object tables indexed by object number × 2 (Obj_Cur): screen position ($0A00), draw buckets ($0E00, 64 words), size class (Obj_SprSize, $1201), draw state (Obj_State, $1B00), position in 1/16 pixel (Obj_PosX/Y), and the event script position.
  • The OAM shadow: low table at $0700 (4 bytes per sprite), high table at $0900, split into three ranges, uploaded by the NMI (Oam_UploadShadow). See How Sprite Init Works.
  • The map page ($1D00, DP=$1D00) for the map code, and the map's metatile buffers in bank $7E/$7F.

docs.title: asar 1.91 Quirks
docs.text:
Surprises in how asar 1.91 picks an instruction's encoding. Future contributors: read this before spending an hour debugging a byte offset.

The short version: asar does not track the M and X flags, and it picks an operand's width from how the operand is written. The project's style rule (STYLE.md) is the fix for all of it: every data instruction whose operand is a define or struct field says .b, .w or .l. With that, every encoding in the matched code is written as an instruction; no opcode bytes are hand-written (db $A9,$7F), and the few encodings that could not be written as an instruction would get a named macro in asm/include/macros.inc (it is empty so far).

Earlier versions of this page recommended raw db bytes, raw BRL offsets and raw hex operands. Those workarounds were wrong or no longer needed (the code repo's STATUS.md records two of them under "Known issues"); the notes below are what the current source does.

docs.title: 1. A label or equate operand assembles as a long address
docs.text:
Symptom: STA INIDISP, where INIDISP = $2100 is an equate (as in asm/hardware.inc), emits opcode 8F (STA long, 4 bytes) instead of 8D (STA absolute, 3 bytes). Everything after it shifts by a byte.

Cause: asar treats a label or equate as a 24-bit address.

Fix: give the width: STA.w INIDISP (8D 00 21). The same goes for STX/STY, which have no long form: plain STX A1T7L is an error ("Unknown command"), while STX.w A1T7L assembles to 8E 72 43. The matched code writes, for example, STX.w A1T7L and STY.w VMADDL.

Defines (!Name = $2100) are textual, so STA !Name takes the width of the number as written ($2100: absolute). The style rule asks for an explicit width on those too, so the encoding cannot drift when a define's value is written differently.

docs.title: 2. Immediate width follows the digits, not the M flag
docs.text:
Symptom: in a 16-bit accumulator section (after REP #$20), LDA #$7F assembles to the 2-byte A9 7F, and the CPU then reads the next byte as the operand's high byte.

Cause: asar doesn't know that M=0. It sizes an immediate by how it is written: #$7F is one byte, #$007F or #$0040 two (SBC #$0040 gives E9 40 00 whatever M is).

Fix: write the width the CPU will use: LDA.w #$007F in 16-bit code, LDA.b #!Bank7F in 8-bit code. The battle number formatters, entered with M=0 by their callers, carry an explicit .w on every SBC/ADC immediate for this reason. (An earlier note blamed asar for "not tracking REP #$20" in SBC/ADC and fixed it with db bytes; the .w suffix alone reproduces those encodings.)

docs.title: 3. Direct page or absolute is chosen the same way
docs.text: STA $01,X assembles as direct page, X (95 01) and STA $0001,X as absolute, X (9D 01 00), again by the digits written. With named operands, use .b for direct page and .w for absolute; code that relocates the direct page onto a register block writes the register relative to its base, as in STA.b INIDISP-!DP_PPU.

docs.title: 4. BRL with a number stores the number as the offset
docs.text:
BRL SomeLabel works: asar computes the 16-bit offset from the next instruction. But BRL $B193 stores $B193 itself as the offset, not as a target address. Write the label.

When the original's offset wraps around the 64 KB bank boundary, the matched code writes the target minus one bank, BRL Target-!BankWrap (!BankWrap = $10000 in asm/include/constants_engine.inc), so asar computes the same wrapped offset; Field_EndOfFrame's tail jump to Oam_BuildShadow is one.

docs.title: 5. Calls to code that is not matched yet
docs.text:
A JSR, JSL or JML to an address outside the matched code needs a name. The project gives each such target a label-only stub in asm/include/unmatched.asm or unmatched_battle.asm: an org to the address and a label, emitting no bytes. When the routine is matched its stub is deleted and the real label takes over. Bank files never hold stubs, and call sites never use raw addresses.

65C816 Assembly
org $C0F05E
Irq_UnkF05E:        ; label only: no bytes emitted

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Situation Wrong Right Store to a named register STA INIDISP (long) STA.w INIDISP STX/STY to a named register STX A1T7L (error) STX.w A1T7L 16-bit immediate LDA #$7F (1-byte operand) LDA.w #$007F 8-bit immediate from a define LDA #!Name LDA.b #!Name Long branch BRL $B193 (raw offset) BRL Label (or Label-!BankWrap across the bank edge) Call into unmatched code JSR $9E29 a stub label in asm/include/unmatched*.asm

docs.title: CI Setup
docs.text: The GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/match.yml in the code repo runs on every pull request to main and every push to main. It has two jobs.

docs.title: Readability standard (no ROM needed)
docs.text:
1. python3 tools/lint_readability.py: every routine outside tools/readability_baseline.txt must meet the readability standard (the header checks that need the ROM are skipped here and run in the second job).
  2. python3 tools/validate_functions.py: the review log in symbols/reviews/ is well formed.
  3. python3 tools/progress.py --check: the generated files (symbols/functions.csv, symbols/progress.json) are not tracked, and no doc carries a generated number.

docs.title: Reassemble and diff (needs the ROM)
docs.text:
1. Restore the ROM from the ROM_B64 secret (see below).
  2. Build asar 1.91 from source and run python3 tools/check_env.py.
  3. make diff: the reassembled ROM must equal the original, byte for byte.
  4. python3 tools/verify.py: every byte the source claims is really emitted by it.
  5. python3 tools/progress.py --update: regenerate symbols/ from the source.
  6. python3 tools/lint_readability.py again, now with the ROM (header and caller checks).
  7. python3 tools/validate_functions.py and python3 tools/progress.py --check again.

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text: Because the ROM cannot be committed to the repo, CI needs it supplied as a GitHub Actions secret encoded in base64.

docs.title: 1. Encode your ROM
docs.text:
Shell
base64 -w 0 roms/chrono_trigger.sfc > /tmp/rom_b64.txt

docs.title: 2. Add it as a repository secret
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions
  2. Click New repository secret
  3. Name: ROM_B64
  4. Value: paste the content of /tmp/rom_b64.txt

The workflow decodes the secret into roms/chrono_trigger.sfc. It also compares the ROM's SHA-256 with the one in docs/ROM_HASH.md when that file exists; the code repo no longer has a docs/ folder, so that comparison is currently skipped. The expected hash is on Target ROM.

docs.title: 3. Verify
docs.text: Open a pull request that touches any .asm file; both checks should appear automatically.

docs.title: If the secret is not set
docs.text: The second job degrades gracefully: it emits a warning and skips everything after restoring the ROM, so it won't fail. The first job always runs. Contributors without the secret can still run everything locally.

docs.title: Local workflow (no CI needed)
docs.text:
Shell
python3 tools/check_env.py   # confirm asar + python3 present
make gate                    # make diff, make verify and make lint in one go
python3 tools/progress.py    # print the current numbers by level and bank

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The code repo's own CONTRIBUTING.md, STYLE.md and REVIEW.md are the rules; this page is a summary of how the work goes.

docs.title: Ways to help
docs.text:
• Bank mapping: identifying what lives where in ROM, even roughly, before anything is matched.
  • Function matching: draft, make readable, gate, review (below).
  • Review: checking routines someone else matched, so they reach verified.
  • Tooling: diffing, cross-references, progress tracking, CI.
  • Data and graphics cataloguing: identifying compressed blobs, tile data and their formats (separate from code matching, but needed eventually).

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
• No ROM data, headers or extracted assets in commits. Ever. Tools and source only.
  • Matched, readable and reviewed, or not on main. A literal transcription of the disassembly is fine on a work branch, never on main.
  • Byte-exact means byte-exact. A routine that "looks equivalent" but doesn't reassemble identically isn't matched.
  • Say how you know. A name or meaning that is inferred says so, and from what ("inferred: only written by the revive path"); an unknown one stays an Unk name or is hedged ("probably"). Community documents and other disassemblies are leads, not evidence.
  • Keep the original's quirks. Dead code, a redundant instruction, an apparent bug: kept, named and documented, never "fixed".
  • No generated numbers in docs. Counts and percentages come from tools/progress.py; never type one by hand, and never commit symbols/functions.csv or symbols/progress.json.
  • One pull request per logical unit: a cluster of routines, a tooling change. Bring a branch up to date by merging main, never by rebasing.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
1. Pick the next target from the code repo's NEXT.md.
  2. Draft it: make draft ADDR=C1:3714 (tools/draft.py) disassembles the routine, tracking M/X, DP and DB, and writes asar source with a header skeleton and every operand the project already has a name for, then checks it assembles to the original bytes. make xref ADDR=... (tools/xref.py) lists every call or jump to an address.
  3. Make it readable (STYLE.md): named RAM (asm/include/ram_*.inc), structs, calls and constants; explicit .b/.w/.l widths (see asar Quirks); no hand-encoded opcodes; a header with what the routine is for and its CPU state on entry and exit (M, X, DP, DB). Calls into unmatched code go through label-only stubs in asm/include/unmatched*.asm.
  4. Generate the Callers blocks: python3 tools/callers.py --update rewrites the ; Callers block of every header from tools/xref.py's confirmed call sites. The block is generated, not reviewed, and left out of the source hash; run it after matching code and after merging main. Hand-written remarks about callers go on a ; Callers note: line.
  5. Gate: make gate runs make diff (byte-exact), make verify (every byte the source claims is really emitted by it) and make lint (tools/lint_readability.py, including the header rules HEADER, CALLERS, SIZE, UNMATCHED and DPDB).
  6. Review: someone who did not write the routine checks a whole cluster against the ROM: every claim true, the CPU state right, names that don't mislead, unknowns hedged. The verdict is one row per routine in a new round file, symbols/reviews/rNNN.csv (address,name,date,reviewer,verdict,source_hash,notes), with the routine's source_hash from symbols/functions.csv. Any later edit to the routine changes its hash and sends it back for review. tools/progress.py --update then marks it verified.
  7. Session end: tools/end_session.sh.

A change to STYLE.md or to the lint's rules is its own commit, approved by the maintainer and logged under "Decisions" in STATUS.md, so no routine is judged by a rule its own author just wrote.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. python3 tools/check_env.py to confirm your toolchain (asar 1.91, Python 3.10+, make).
  2. Drop your own legally dumped ROM in roms/chrono_trigger.sfc (never committed; see Target ROM).
  3. make diff should report a 100% match.

How much of the game's code is matched, and how far each routine has come. Every figure on this page is generated when the site is built; nothing here is typed by hand.

A routine moves through three levels, each including the one before:

  • matched: every byte from its label to the next is emitted by the source and equals the original ROM (make diff, and make verify, which assembles onto blank bases so a routine can't hide behind original bytes);
  • readable: it also meets the project's readability standard (named RAM, calls and constants, explicit widths, a header with its CPU state on entry and exit), checked by tools/lint_readability.py;
  • verified: an independent reviewer approved its current source. The approval is a row in a review round file (symbols/reviews/rNNN.csv) that carries the routine's source hash, so any later edit to the routine sends it back for review.

The share of code is measured against the roughly 358 KB of the 4 MB ROM that is 65816 code; the rest is graphics, music, maps and text. The source also emits data (tables, $FF fill, leftovers of an older build): each routine in functions.csv has a kind, data when its source is only db/dw/dl/fill lines, and the share counts code bytes alone, with the data bytes shown beside it. A bank's code size comes from a one-off survey until its source covers the whole bank, then from the source itself (bank $C0); a bank whose matched code outgrows its survey is measured against the matched figure and marked "survey low".

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
The code repository's tools/progress.py builds the source, proves which bytes it emits, applies the readability lint and the review log, and writes symbols/functions.csv and symbols/progress.json (generated, never committed there). The wiki's tools/sync_progress.py copies them, with the day-by-day history, into docs/data/, and the site renders them.

The routines themselves are listed on each system page and in the slice pop-ups of the ROM Map.

docs.title: How the cartridge is laid out
docs.text:
The US 1.0 cartridge is a 4 MB HiROM board: 64 banks of 64 KB, $400000 bytes in all. The CPU can see the same ROM bytes at several addresses:

CPU banks What they show $C0–$FF The whole 64 KB of every ROM bank. These are the canonical addresses this wiki uses. $40–$7D The same banks again, minus the last two: $7E–$7F are work RAM instead. $00–$3F The upper half ($8000–$FFFF) of each bank; the lower half is RAM and hardware registers. $80–$BF A mirror of $00–$3F, used to select the faster ROM access speed.

So $C0:FF00 and $00:FF00 are the same byte, which is why the reset code, the internal header and the interrupt vectors at the top of bank $C0 are often written with bank $00. A file offset is (bank − $C0) × $10000 + address: $C1:0089 is at 0x010089 in the ROM file.

Only about 358 KB of the 4 MB is 65C816 code; the rest is graphics, music, maps and text, built from the original bytes. The code size of each bank comes from a one-off survey of a reference disassembly, which marked every byte as code or data, except where the source covers the whole bank ($C0): there it is the bytes of the routines that are code, not tables or fill.

  • Game loop and location loading ($C0:0000–$C0:0B85): ReentryVectors, GameLoop, GameLoop_FrameBody, Field_EndOfFrame, LoadLocation and its steps, the field save and restore around bank-$C2 calls, and the field/battle hand-off ($C0:0283–$C0:0904).
  • Scene changes and the field frame ($C0:0B86–$C0:2E66): Field_InitLoadState, Field_SceneChangeTick with the tile-animation handlers ModeE6_Handler … ModeFC_Handler and DefaultHandler, pause and menu input, the action button, the services ReentryVectors offers other banks, the fades, the message window step, the 16 window-effect hooks, the staff credits, the tile-animation list, the layer 2/3 drift steps, and ClearRAMDMA.
  • Event script opcodes ($C0:2E67–$C0:56A5, $C0:5F6E–$C0:6D2E), the object scheduler and init ($C0:56A6–$C0:5D6D) and the opcode table Evt_OpcodeTable ($C0:5D6E).
  • Graphics, palettes and slots ($C0:6D2F–$C0:7398): location graphics packs, VRAM and CGRAM uploads, and the tile-slot and palette-slot allocators.
  • The map ($C0:7399–$C0:A80F): map set-up, layer redraws and edge builders, the edge uploads, Field_FrameUpdate and the D-pad, the leader's collision and tile effects, the layer scroll, and the party members' steps and animations ($C0:9E29–$C0:A33A).
  • Objects and sprites ($C0:A810–$C0:EA62): object motion and view culling, the draw buckets, Oam_BuildShadow and the sprite placement routines, the animation tick and frame-build queue, the frame builders, Spr_LoadLargeObj and the tile buffer allocators.
  • NMI ($C0:EA63–$C0:ECCB): NmiHandler, Field_WaitFrame, Credits_UploadLine and Oam_UploadShadow.
  • IRQ ($C0:ECCC–$C0:F16F): IrqHandler, Irq_UploadTileAnim, and the message choice cursor it draws (Irq_DrawChoiceCursor and the row clears Irq_ChoiceCursorClearRow0–3).
  • Leftovers ($C0:F170–$C0:F2FF): BankC0_OldBuildLeftovers, not code and, as far as found, never read: copies of the tails of the choice-cursor code just before it, "probably what earlier, longer assemblies of this part of the bank left behind", then $FF fill.
  • Tables and the top of the bank: Rom_AngleTable ($C0:F300, the direction of a vector for run and rise 0–31, 256 steps per turn), Rom_DirToFacing ($C0:F700, the facing up, down, left or right for each direction), Rom_SineTable256 ($C0:F800, signed sine, 256 steps per turn) and Rom_SineTable ($C0:F900, |sin| for 1024 steps per turn), read by the field, battle and scene code; then BitReverseTable ($C0:FD00), RandomTable ($C0:FE00, probably the game's random bytes: a shuffle of 0–255), then Reset, the interrupt stubs, BitSet / BitClear, the wave tables, the cartridge header and the vectors ($C0:FF00 on).

See Engine core, Field event scripts, Frame cycle and NMI, Sprites & objects and Boot.

Nearly every byte of bank $C1 is code, and almost all of it is the battle. It opens with entry vectors and a same-bank service dispatcher ($C1:0000–$C1:0050, not matched yet). Also open are the behaviour-script handlers ($C1:8EAB–$C1:AC13) and the code after the long veneers ($C1:FDD3 on). Matched:

  • $C1:007E–$C1:1F78: the frame wait, maths and shift helpers, number formatting, trig, the status bar, the battle menu with its tech and item lists and ready queue, and the battler frame decoder.
  • $C1:1F79–$C1:4057: targeting, battler boxes and collision, the position queries, the PC and enemy animation ticks, status effects, poses and the enemy movers.
  • $C1:4058–$C1:7FFF: service 4 and the action scripts (loaders, path search, threads, every opcode handler and their tables), then BankC1_OldBuildLeftovers ($C1:7C3D: not code, the cut-off remains of older assemblies of some of those tables, then $FF fill).
  • $C1:8000 on: BattleSys_Main, the turn lists, the enemy behaviour script core and its tables, the battler checks, the turn helpers, the PC command runner, the target resolution, the tech menus and MP costs, the inventory and gold services, the effect types and their arithmetic (hit roll, damage, statuses, drain, steal), the 16-bit maths and random ranges, the hit records, the battle-end status clears, the hit modifiers ($C1:ED89–$C1:F204), the experience, levels and tech points ($C1:F205–$C1:FA60), Battle_SetupBattle and the long veneers for bank $FD.

See Battle engine and the battle pages it links to.

The scene half, $C2:0000–$C2:7FFF, is matched: the entry vectors, the scene mode's boot, NMI, VRAM queue, tasks, BG layer scrolls and redraws, sprite list, animation and scene scripts with all their ops, the mode handlers, scene loading, sound zones, the watchers and the party and object tasks, the direction helpers, the text decoder ($C2:57DF–$C2:6262), the map view and dial of modes 6 and 8, the screen effects and script routines with the extra-graphics loaders ($C2:754D–$C2:7DE3), and $FF fill up to $C2:8000. From the menu half: the entry vectors at $C2:8000, the menu's entry, thread scheduler, fades and VRAM queue ($C2:800E–$C2:840D), its NMI and IRQ handlers, the joypad reader and play-time clock ($C2:840E–$C2:85D5), the uploads, inventory, character and item helpers, cursors and list arrows ($C2:8663–$C2:8C35), and the PPU, RAM and new-game set-up ($C2:940D–$C2:960A). The menu's screens are not matched yet. See Scene engine, Menu and Text windows.
