For comparison, all of bank $C0 matched so far (19,498 bytes) is about 31.6% of its bank; at today's start, bank $C1 looked like a multi-year project on its own.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Bank $C1 has three broad areas: math and number formatting ($C1:0089–$C1:02xx), BattleUI and BattleMenu ($C1:02xx–$C1:1xxx), and enemy logic, animation and phase control ($C1:1xxx–$C1:FFFF, including EnemyAI_SpatialService at $C1:2986, a fully documented, isolated routine in the reference). The next neighbor is BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL at $C1:10E3, the target of the entry vector at $C10012 (BattleSys_EntryVec12 in the dscotton reference): the dirty-flag gate that decides whether UpdateWindows runs at all. After it, the cursor-movement and input layer that starts around $C1:106E.

docs.title: 19 September 2026: the battle command menu, from dirty flag to committed action
docs.text: The biggest single day so far: 1,478 bytes in 22 routines, all in bank $C1's battle command menu. It now runs as matched code from the gate that decides whether to redraw the menu, through controller input and confirm, to the 8-byte action record the battle engine executes. This is the first stretch of session 41, worked in eight increments.

docs.title: The dirty-flag gate
docs.text:
The battle menu doesn't redraw every frame. It waits until something changes, then does one full pass. Two sibling routines gate that pass, both on the WRAM flag $993A:

Text Only
LDA $993A
BEQ <exit>
STZ $993A
STZ $E5
JSR BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler
JSR BattleMenu_UpdateWindows
JSR BattleMenu_ProcessInput
JSR BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay

If the flag is clear they return at once. If it is set they clear it and run the rebuild: pull the next ATB-ready battler into the queue, refresh the window contents (matched on 14 August), process controller input, redraw the cursor overlay.

They differ in how they are reached:

  • BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL ($C1:10E3, 23 bytes) is in the bank's cross-bank entry-vector table. Other banks reach it with JSL $C10012, which JMPs within the bank to $C110E3 without touching the stack, so the routine must return with RTL to match the long call.
  • BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyAndTick ($C1:10FA, 27 bytes) is a plain JSR target, called from several places in the battle-phase state machine. It adds a cross-bank tick (JSL $CD0009) before an ordinary RTS.

Same logic, two calling conventions. Two near-identical routines are not necessarily duplicated code; they can serve call sites with different stack contracts.

Three of those callees weren't matched yet (BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler at $C1:1B67, BattleMenu_ProcessInput at $C1:1153 and BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay at $C1:17DD), so they went in as label stubs: an org line with a bare label and no bytes, the trick used earlier in bank $C0 for forward references. asar resolves the JSRs, and a later increment fills in the body at the same org.

BattleMenu_DrawCursorSprites ($C1:1115, 62 bytes) sits between the gate routines and ProcessInput. It builds the four OAM entries of the cursor that points at the selected command. The shape is a fixed 4-tile template in ROM ($CCF604–$CCF607); the position comes from per-slot coordinates at $1D0C/$1D23, indexed by the active PC. The attribute byte's palette bits are replaced from $9F46 each time, almost certainly what makes the cursor flash or change color. What drives that byte isn't traced yet.

docs.title: Reading the controller
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ProcessInput ($C1:1153, 142 bytes) reads two WRAM bytes, $EE and $EF. They are pad-edge bytes: a bit is set only on the frame a button goes from released to pressed, not while it is held. $EE holds buttons (confirm is $80), $EF the D-pad ($02 left, $08 up, $04 down, $01 right). The routine:

  • no active PC ($95D5 negative): return
  • target-select mode ($9609 != 0, you're aiming at a target): hand over to BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput
  • submenu type $95DB is the tech or item list: hand over to that list's input handler
  • otherwise, the main command menu: check left, up, down, right, confirm, in that order

Each branch ends in a JMP, not a fall-through, so only one fires per frame. If two D-pad bits were somehow set on the same frame, only the first checked (left) would act. The hardware makes that close to impossible, but the dispatch is exclusive, not layered.

Four small leaves:

  • BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev ($C1:11E1, 55 bytes) and BattleMenu_CycleActivePcNext ($C1:1218, 56 bytes), for left and right, decrement or increment the active-PC index $A6DD, wrapping across the party (0..2). They skip any slot whose $A6D9 entry is negative (fainted or unavailable) by repeating until they land on a valid one. Both carry the cursor row ($95DC) from the old slot to the new one, so switching characters keeps your place in the menu.
  • BattleMenu_CursorUp ($C1:1250, 20 bytes) and BattleMenu_CursorDown ($C1:1264, 23 bytes) move $95DC for the active PC, wrapping over the three rows, and set a redraw flag ($A43F) so the cursor sprite moves next frame.

A branch that probably never runs. Both cycle routines branch on $A0D4 right after finding the new slot. Clear (normal): copy the cursor row across. Set: read a per-PC default row from $9916 and write it to the old slot's $95DC (through Y instead of X), which looks backwards. The reference disassembly flags this path as unreachable in the shipped game, and the odd target fits: leftover logic from an earlier version. It is reproduced byte for byte. The goal is a ROM that reassembles identically, oddities included.

Two borrowed leaves. Battle_ZeroResultEE ($C1:179C, 5 bytes) is STZ $EE, STZ $EF, RTS: the shared exit for nearly every routine here, clearing both pad-edge bytes once the input is used. Battle_StopSfx ($C1:1B55, 18 bytes) plays (or, by its name, cancels) a sound on cursor moves and confirms by writing $1E00–$1E02 and calling JSL $C70004, exactly like Sub_1B90 in bank $C0. The audio-command protocol is the same across the engine.

The same increment closed a tooling gap: tools/progress.py --update-index now syncs mkdocs.yml's stats block and index.md's matched-regions table from PROGRESS.md, instead of both being hand-edited every session (which had already drifted more than once).

docs.title: Pressing confirm
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ConfirmCommand ($C1:127B, 33 bytes) reloads the active-PC pointer, reads that PC's cursor row (0, 1 or 2: Attack, Tech, Item) and tail-jumps to the matching handler. On the way it writes $FF to $A0D7. Nothing here reads it back, but the reference shows it compared inside BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame, so it is probably a marker that forces a status-bar refresh next time.

  • BattleMenu_ChooseAttack ($C1:129C, 32 bytes, row 0) sets the target mode $960D to $07, calls the target-list builder, and increments $9609, the flag ProcessInput checks first. Confirming Attack doesn't open a submenu. It changes what the next frame's input handler means.
  • BattleMenu_OpenTechList ($C1:12BC, 49 bytes, row 1) and BattleMenu_OpenItemList ($C1:12ED, 51 bytes, row 2) render their lists (with the routines matched on 14 August), set the submenu type $95DB and return. The item version also copies a fixed $180-byte graphic into the command-window tilemap. The reference calls it ItemBoxBattles, in bank $D1 next to the TechBoxBattles graphic that BattleMenu_LoadCommandWindowMap uses. Presumably the item list needs a different border. Both gate on a flag at $A0A7 that reads like "list locked"; what would lock it (a status effect? a command restriction?) isn't clear, so it is a loose end.

docs.title: Building the target list
docs.text:
BattleMenu_BuildTargetList ($C1:1F79, 100 bytes) is what ChooseAttack calls. According to the reference, the tech-confirm and item-confirm paths call it too, so it is a shared dependency for three submenus.

It resets a handful of target-selection variables and fills two 11-entry lists, candidates and selection, with $FF. Eleven fits the layout: 3 party members plus up to 8 enemies. If target-select isn't already active in a "return here on cancel" state, it saves the current submenu type to $A86B before clearing it, so cancelling brings you back to the menu you were in (main, tech or item) instead of the top.

Then it clamps the target mode $960D into range, doubles it into a word index and jumps through a table: JSR ($1FF8,X). Each entry is a handler that knows how to collect targets for one mode (Attack, an area tech, a party-wide heal...). That table and its dozen-plus handlers (BattleTgt_CollectValidTargets, BattleTgt_ListEnemiesSingle and others in the reference) are a separate subsystem. BuildTargetList refers to the table by raw address and stops there, the same deferral used for bank $C0's $5D6E entity table.

The bug. An early draft put LDA #$FF inside the clearing loop:

Text Only
; wrong
.clear_loop:
    LDA #$FF
    STA $99C0,X
    STA $A62D,X
    DEX
    BPL .clear_loop

The ROM loads it once, before:

Text Only
; correct
LDA #$FF
.clear_loop:
    STA $99C0,X
    STA $A62D,X
    DEX
    BPL .clear_loop

Both behave the same, but moving the load changes where the loop starts, so the BPL offset changes. make diff flagged one byte at $C1:1F9C, the offset byte. Byte-exact matching checks the encoding, not just the logic: a change any reviewer would call "obviously equivalent" still fails, at once.

docs.title: The ready queue
docs.text:
ATB means battlers act when their gauge fills, not in strict turns, so several can become ready in the same frame or while the menu is busy. BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler ($C1:1B67, 67 bytes) handles that with a 3-slot FIFO at WRAM $95D6-$95D9 and a count at $95DA. Dequeuing:

  • restores the battler's saved cursor row (if you left it on "Item", it's still on "Item")
  • marks the slot present in the active roster
  • shifts the remaining entries down one
  • if nobody is the active menu PC, makes this battler the active one

One line looks odd out of context: STA $A6D9,X with A and X both holding the slot's own index. Elsewhere today $A6D9,X is a presence check (BMI after loading it means "slot empty"). Writing the slot's index there is the "occupied" marker, not a translation table.

The shift reads $95D8 twice, writing it to $95D7 and then $95D9, instead of reading $95D9 for the second write. Since the count never exceeds 3, it probably never matters, and it is reproduced as is. This closed the last stub callee of the dirty-flag gate.

BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady ($C1:1BAA, 144 bytes), next door, is the inverse. A battler may be waiting in the queue or already promoted to the active menu character, and it tells them apart by $A6D9,X (negative: not promoted). From the queue it scans for the entry and shifts the rest down, starting anywhere, not just at the head. For the active PC it also has to leave the menu in a sane state:

  • cancel target selection ($9609 and a couple of related flags)
  • reset the submenu type to the main menu ($95DB)
  • clear the battler's roster slot
  • search the roster for another battler to promote, or explicitly set "no active PC" if there is none, so $A6DD/$95D5 never point at stale data

The same bug, again. An early draft put a one-time load (LDA $80, the slot to search for) inside the scan loop. make diff flagged one byte on the loop's closing branch, as with BuildTargetList. A lone one-byte diff on a branch operand near loop code is now my first guess.

docs.title: Target-select input
docs.text:
BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput ($C1:1561, 185 bytes) reads the controller while you point at an enemy or ally. Unlike the main menu, it calls BattleMenu_BuildTargetList on every call, because valid targets can change mid-selection (an enemy can die from a status tick). If the rebuild finds no target, or you cancel, it leaves target-select and restores the previous menu (main, tech or item), repainting its window as needed. Otherwise it polls the pad: confirm tail-jumps to BattleMenu_CommitAction; the D-pad cycles forward or backward through targets, unless the mode targets everyone, which disables cycling.

Eighteen bytes that never run. In the middle of the cancel path is something shaped like a second copy of the item-window graphic loader: same source table, same destination. But its loop branch points forward, into the confirm/cycle section, not back to itself. If it ran it would copy one byte and leave, nowhere near the 384 bytes the working copy loop elsewhere in the routine moves. And nothing reaches it: every path before it ends in an unconditional branch past it. These are bytes the CPU can never execute under any input or game state. The single orphaned RTS on 14 August was the only dead code seen before; this is the first dead multi-instruction block. The likely story is a branch target changed during development and the old live code left behind. Either way, it is reproduced exactly.

docs.title: Committing the action
docs.text:
Every confirm press ends in BattleMenu_CommitAction ($C1:161A, 308 bytes), the largest routine in the command-menu cluster. It builds a uniform 8-byte record, "character X does Y to target Z", whether Y is an attack, a tech or an item. It dispatches on $95DB to fill in the parts that differ, then joins shared code that writes the record and hands off. Attack is almost trivial: a type flag and a marker for "no tech or item id". Item decrements the item's stock and clears some UI scroll state. Tech is the interesting one, because dual and triple techs involve more than one character.

BattleMenu_ConsumePartnerSlot ($C1:174E, 30 bytes) takes a combo partner out of the turn pool so it doesn't also act on its own later: it clears the slot's presence in the active roster (decrementing the active-PC count if it was on screen) and clears a flag bit on that battler's sprite data (called the "queued" bit at the time). CommitAction calls it once for a dual tech's partner (low nibble of $9EE7) and again for a second partner only if the high nibble says triple tech. The combo bookkeeping was built to scale from two to three, not bolted on.

Then the same cleanup seen in RemoveBattlerFromReady: clear the confirming character's slot, then find another active menu character or mark "no active PC".

BattleMenu_TargetNext ($C1:176C, 26 bytes) and BattleMenu_TargetPrev ($C1:1786, 22 bytes) move the target cursor through valid targets, skipping invalid slots, with the same wrap-and-retry shape as CycleActivePcPrev/Next. TargetPrev has no RTS of its own: it sits right before Battle_ZeroResultEE and runs into it.

With CommitAction, everything from the dirty-flag gate to a confirmed target is one unbroken span of matched code. Working a cluster in order pays off: callees stop being stubs one by one until the whole subsystem is visible.

docs.title: Fixing the progress bookkeeping
docs.text:
Before any code, the standing staleness audit (checking that PROGRESS.md's headline, its per-bank headings and the generated homepage snippet agree) found two real bugs. The bank $C0 heading had read 384 bytes low since session 33, when that session's total went in without updating it. And tools/progress.py choked on comma-formatted byte counts, so bank $C1 had been missing from the generated summary since it opened. Both are fixed: the heading corrected, and the parser strips commas before converting.

Right after the first routines, the same class of bug came back: the bank $C1 table got its new rows, but the heading's byte count didn't move until the audit ran again. Twice in one sitting means a process gap, not a slip; the fix belongs in tooling, which is what the --update-index change above does.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Two submenu-input stubs remain: BattleMenu_TechListInput and BattleMenu_ItemListInput, which mirror each other and TargetSelectInput. Behind them, per the reference, sit routines like BattleMenu_TechConfirm and an item-confirm equivalent. Also still open: BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay ($C1:17DD), the 117-byte periodic/idle-check service at $C1:106E, and the target-mode handler table at $C1:1FF8, a dozen-plus BattleTgt_* handlers referenced only by address so far, which deserves a session of its own.

docs.title: 22 September 2026: the tech and item lists, and the command menu is closed
docs.text: The input handling for the tech list and the item list is matched, the last two submenus still holding stubs. Every input handler in the battle command menu is now matched code. 637 bytes in 15 routines, the last two increments of session 41.

docs.title: The tech list: one cursor, two coordinate systems
docs.text:
BattleMenu_TechListInput ($C1:1320, 73 bytes) runs every frame the tech list is open. It works out which entry is highlighted (scroll position plus cursor row), then checks the pad for confirm, cancel or a direction. BattleMenu_TechConfirm ($C1:1369, 38 bytes) hands over to targeting, like BattleMenu_ChooseAttack does for Attack. BattleMenu_TechListCancel ($C1:138F, 30 bytes) restores the cursor and scroll saved before the list opened and goes back to the main menu.

Not every tech in the list is selectable. A character may not have learned it, or may not have the MP. Those entries carry an availability flag, and the cursor must skip them. But two things are being tracked: the tech's index in the underlying list, and where the cursor sits on screen (a row 0–2 plus a scroll offset). Press up when the previous entry is unavailable, and the cursor has to move to the next available entry, which may be two or three list slots away.

BattleMenu_TechListPrev ($C1:13AD, 71 bytes) and BattleMenu_TechListNext ($C1:13F4, 73 bytes) solve it by counting. Each walks the list index one step at a time, checking the flag, until it reaches a selectable entry, and counts the steps. Then it replays that count on the screen position (row and scroll), scrolling the window by a row whenever the cursor would leave the visible part. Two loops, same shape, same count, applied to two representations of "where you are". The list walk finds out how far you moved; the screen replay trusts the number without needing to know why. The availability flags are only checked once.

docs.title: The item list: almost the tech list, but simpler
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ItemListInput ($C1:143D, 91 bytes) has the same confirm/cancel/up/down checks plus two branches the tech list lacks: page the list up or down three rows at once, and a check of a flag ($A0D0) that forces a full re-render when something elsewhere has marked the display stale.

Cursor movement is where it differs most. Items don't need skipping: an unusable item still gets a cursor position and just renders greyed out. So BattleMenu_ItemCursorUp ($C1:14EC, 22 bytes) and BattleMenu_ItemCursorDown ($C1:1502, 26 bytes) move the row by one and only call a scroll helper at the top or bottom edge of the window. Same UI pattern, different implementation, because the two lists have different rules for where the cursor may stop.

Borrowing another routine's ending. BattleMenu_ItemListPageDown ($C1:151C, 27 bytes) and BattleMenu_ItemListPageUp ($C1:1537, 20 bytes) don't call the renderer themselves. They set the scroll position and JSR into the middle of BattleMenu_ItemListScrollDown ($C1:17BF, 30 bytes) / BattleMenu_ItemListScrollUp ($C1:17A1, 30 bytes), right at the instruction that calls the renderer, so that routine's tail (render, then flag the scroll arrows for a refresh) does double duty. Bank $C0's Sub_1BA7 does the same, entering Sub_1B90 partway to reuse its tail. On the matching side, that internal entry point had to be a real global label instead of a private .dot label: in asar a new global label resets the local scope, so a label jumped to from outside must be global.

A branch that can't happen. BattleMenu_ItemListScrollUp opens with two BEQs in a row on the same flag, with nothing in between that changes it. The first is a normal check. The second asks a question already answered: if the flag were set, the first branch would have fired. This is a different kind of "does nothing" from the dead block in BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput three days ago. That was code nothing can execute; this runs every time and always gets "no". Both are reproduced exactly.

BattleMenu_ItemConfirm ($C1:1498, 67 bytes), BattleMenu_ItemListCancel ($C1:14DB, 17 bytes) and BattleMenu_ItemListRefresh ($C1:154B, 22 bytes) complete the set.

docs.title: Fixing an old label
docs.text: Working out an item record for ItemConfirm (id, target mode, flags, quantity, in that order, five bytes apart) showed that BattleMenu_RenderItemRow, matched on 14 August, had two field comments backwards: it called the quantity field "item ID" and the id field an "unconfirmed-animation flag". That routine only reads the fields; ItemConfirm's branches reveal what they mean. The old comments are corrected. No bytes changed.

docs.title: What this closes
docs.text: Every submenu the command window can open, the main Attack/Tech/Item menu, the tech list, the item list and target selection, now has matched input handling and confirm logic, and the tech and item lists have matched navigation. Together with the confirm dispatch and command commit from 19 September, the whole path from "the menu needs a redraw" to "a battle command has been built and queued" is byte-exact end to end.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay at $C1:17DD, the last single-routine stub in this neighborhood. After that, the target-mode handlers behind $C1:1FF8, and the much larger territory past $C1:1C4A: enemy logic, battle animation and most of the 481 routines scouted when the bank opened.

docs.title: 24 September 2026: the cursor that draws itself
docs.text: One big routine: BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay, 828 bytes, the last stub in the command-menu neighborhood. Every frame, after input is processed, it decides what the pointing hand (or hands) on screen should look like, and where.

docs.title: One routine, four jobs
docs.text: It starts with dispatch. If no party member is choosing a command, hide the cursor and stop. If the player is picking a target, draw target cursors. Otherwise branch on the open submenu: main, tech or item. The main menu path does nothing: its cursor was already drawn earlier in the frame by BattleMenu_DrawCursorSprites, so it skips to the end. The other three paths each solve a different problem, so it reads like four small routines stitched together.

docs.title: Dual and triple techs get more than one hand
docs.text:
Combo techs need the cursor to show who is involved. The tech path checks the highlighted tech's id. Below $39 it is a single-character tech and gets one hand. At $39 and above, it reads a byte that packs the partners into two nibbles (low nibble first partner, high nibble second, $F meaning nobody) and places one cursor over the caster and one over each partner.

Every placement uses the same formula: the battler's base screen position, plus a second per-battler offset (probably the live animated position), minus 16 to center the sprite. It appears six times, unrolled each time instead of in a helper. On a 3.58 MHz CPU, saving a JSR/RTS per cursor was apparently worth the bytes.

docs.title: The item list only redraws when it has to
docs.text:
The item path manages the up/down scroll arrows and the row highlight, and keeps a cached copy of the last value drawn for each. If the live value matches the cache, nothing is touched. Only on a change does it redraw, and only then does it ask for the tile buffer to be uploaded to video memory.

At the top of the list the up arrow is hidden; at the bottom (scroll position $FA) the down arrow is hidden. When the down arrow is visible it uses attribute $A9 instead of the usual $29, unlike the up arrow. That looks deliberate: "more below" gets the emphasis, "more above" doesn't.

docs.title: Picking a target, and "target all"
docs.text:
Single-target selection draws one cursor over the chosen battler. Only in the plain Attack menu, and only when the target is an enemy, it goes through one of two cross-bank message calls that drive the enemy info panel. A per-enemy flag table at $E1DE80 decides whether the panel gets the real target id or $FF. Neither callee is matched yet, so their exact behavior is a guess.

Multi-target selection took the longest to understand. There are only four cursor sprites, but a "hit everything" tech can target more battlers than that. The routine doesn't draw them all in one frame. It scans the selection list three entries at a time, saves where it stopped ($960B), and continues from there next frame, wrapping to the start after six. The cursors alternate between groups of targets on successive frames: limited sprites, so the work and the drawing are spread across frames, a trade-off the SNES forces on many games.

docs.title: Matching notes
docs.text: Nothing exotic, but the size made bookkeeping matter. There are forty-two local .labels, all branch targets inside this one routine. Several branches are just out of 8-bit range, so the original uses a short branch to a nearby JMP. Those trampolines (.tech_single_jmp, .to_tail and others) have to sit exactly where they are, or every address after them shifts.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The command menu has no stubs left. The next piece is the target-mode handler table at $C1:1FF8, a dozen-plus BattleTgt_* routines the menu calls but that are only referenced by address so far. First a small gap: $C1:1B19–$C1:1B54, between this routine and Battle_StopSfx.

docs.title: 8 October 2026: who can you hit? The target modes
docs.text:
The code that answers "who does this action hit?" for the battle menu is matched: a 33-entry table of target modes and the eighteen small routines behind it, plus the routine that puts a character into the ready queue. 1,033 bytes in 26 functions (session 43).

Cyclone hits whoever is near the enemy you picked. Aura heals one ally. Luminaire hits everyone. Every action ends with that question, and this is the code that answers it.

docs.title: Joining the queue
docs.text:
BattleMenu_EnqueueReadyBattler ($C1:1B19–$C1:1B54, 60 bytes) is the opposite of DequeueReadyBattler from 19 September. Nothing calls it by address, which was confusing at first. The answer is the small service table at the top of the bank: code calls $C10045 with a service number, and service 1 is this routine; service 2 is RemoveBattlerFromReady. I first guessed that other banks used the table. A later review searched the whole ROM and found that every call to it is a JSR from inside bank $C1 itself. So it is the battle engine's own internal dispatcher, not a door for other banks.

It does four things:

  1. skips characters already in the active roster
  2. sets a "waiting for a command" bit on the character
  3. appends the character to the queue and resets their menu cursor to its default row
  4. plays a sound through the same audio command as Battle_PlaySfx0 (then called Battle_StopSfx), with sound id $42, very likely the "turn ready" cue

That bit fixed an old mistake. ConsumePartnerSlot's comments called bit 7 of that flag byte the "queued" bit. Now that I can see what sets it, bit 7 means "waiting for a command", and bit 6 (set by CommitAction) means "command queued". The comments are corrected; no bytes changed.

docs.title: Thirty-three modes, eighteen routines
docs.text:
The target-mode table (BattleTgt_ModeTable, $C1:1FF8–$C1:2039) has 33 entries but only 18 distinct handlers, and 12 of the 33 point at the default "pick one ally" handler. That looks like room left for modes nobody needed.

The simple modes share one list builder. Each picks a slot range (allies 0–2, enemies 3–10), optionally sets "target everything", and jumps into BattleTgt_CollectValidTargets. It walks the range and keeps each battler that is present, not flagged out and not hidden. A battler marked KO'd only gets in when the mode is $04. If the caster is in range, they always go first, so when you heal, the cursor starts on yourself.

A few modes are more particular:

  • Self: just the active character. Three instructions.
  • KO'd ally: an unrolled check of each party member's status byte for the "down" bit. That is the revive target list.
  • A specific character: two modes search the party for one character id (4 and 5) and target only them. If that character isn't in the party or can't be targeted, the mode reports "no target". This is how a combo tech can insist on a particular partner.

docs.title: Area attacks
docs.text:
The other modes are area modes, and they share one recipe:

  1. Pick an anchor: the caster, an enemy you aim at, or a party member found by character id.
  2. Fill a small parameter block: source, aim point, a shape/size code and a variant flag.
  3. Call a geometry routine that works out who is inside the area.
  4. Select the whole result.

The enemy-anchored modes still let you move the cursor. Watching the pad bits shows a quirk: the three "line from the caster to the enemy" modes step the cursor forward whether you press left/up or right/down, while the other area modes step backward for one of the two. I don't know yet whether players ever notice.

The radius modes use two size codes, and one mode in each pair swaps in a bigger one ($19): two different techs sharing a handler, told apart by mode number.

The geometry routines (four of them, roughly 1.1 KB from $C1:2332) aren't matched yet. For now they are label stubs, so the handlers can call them by name.

docs.title: A second door into the same room
docs.text: BattleTgt_RunAreaQuery is service 7 in the same service table. It is a 13-byte dispatcher with its own 7-entry table pointing at the same four geometry routines ($C1:1FDD–$C1:1FF7 together). So the menu isn't the only thing asking "who is in this area?". Other code in the battle engine asks too, most likely for enemy attacks, which need the same answer.

docs.title: Little things
docs.text:
• BattleTgt_CycleNext/CyclePrev duplicate the menu's TargetNext/TargetPrev (19 September) instead of sharing them.
  • BattleTgt_EnemyArea2332 has a dead RTS after its final JMP. Nothing reaches it, but it is in the ROM, so it is in the source.
  • BattleTgt_ClearLists blanks 12 entries of lists that only ever use 11.

docs.title: A better check
docs.text: Building on top of the original ROM has one blind spot: if a routine somehow didn't get written at all, the original bytes would still be there and make diff would report a match. So I also rebuilt over a copy of the ROM with every newly matched range zeroed first, and compared again. All 1,033 bytes came back from source.

docs.title: Readable before it counts
docs.text:
The rest of the day changed what "done" means. Until now a routine was finished once its bytes matched. From today, there are three levels, and only the last one counts as done:

  1. Matched: the source assembles to the exact bytes of the ROM.
  2. Readable: the source passes tools/lint_readability.py. Named structures instead of raw offsets (SprTile[3].OfsY or !Pc_MenuRow,X, not a bare address), named calls instead of addresses, named constants for anything that isn't obviously a count, an explicit .b/.w/.l width wherever asar can't know it, and no test plumbing inside the game's code.
  3. Verified: someone other than the author read the routine against the ROM and approved it. The approval is tied to a hash of the routine's source, header comments included, so editing a single comment sends the routine back for review.

The gate went into the pre-commit hook the same evening. Then every routine written so far was brought up to it: bank $C0, bank $C1, the boot code in $FD and the vectors in $00. All 256 routines (29,032 bytes) are now readable, and the readability baseline file, which listed the routines still waiting, is empty.

Review is the slow part, and that's how it should be. Each reviewer gets only the source, the ROM and the style guide, and checks every comment against the bytes. The first two rounds turned up real mistakes:

  • The OBSEL decode was wrong.
  • The "TP gauge" is the ATB gauge.
  • The sine table holds 1,024 one-byte entries, not 512 words.
  • The tech header text in the ROM reads "Double Technique" and "Triple Technique".
  • Three target-mode headers claimed bytes that belong to the routine after them.

The second round of bank $C1 mostly asks for the same thing everywhere: every header must state the direct page, because the code clears A with TDC and that only works because D is 0. 68 routines are verified so far. The rest are going through another round of fixes.

All the numbers on this wiki now come from one script, tools/progress.py, instead of being kept by hand. The first time it ran, it showed that bank $C0 had been over-counted by 169 bytes.

docs.title: Faster, and in parallel
docs.text:
By the afternoon all 244 earlier routines were verified, so the workflow itself got an overhaul. Seven new tools:

  • tools/xref.py finds every real caller of an address and ignores false hits inside other instructions' operands.
  • The lint now insists that every header has Entry and Exit lines and a complete list of callers. Reviews used to send most routines back for exactly those gaps.
  • REVIEW.md writes down the review standard, so every round applies the same bar.
  • A duplicate finder that ignores jump and call addresses.
  • A data-table tool.
  • tools/draft.py, which turns any address into a draft that already assembles byte-for-byte and already uses every name the project knows.

With those, three matchers ran at once in different banks, each batch reviewed by subsystem before it went in. Most batches passed review on the first try.

What they found:

  • Enemy movement ($C1:3714–$C1:4057, 2,372 bytes). A routine stubbed as "status effect visuals" turned out to drive how enemies move. Nine movers: approach, charge, keep range on a ring, orbit, loop round an ellipse, line up on a row or column, eight fixed directions, head for the screen centre, and idle.
  • Battle position queries and collision boxes, plus the battler frame decoder and the PC and enemy animation ticks. One routine in there has a real bug in the original game: a check that is supposed to measure the path to another battler compares against a value left over from the sine lookup instead.
  • The field main loop's per-frame work ($C0, 1,882 bytes). It includes the window effects that shrink and grow the screen, the action button, and the staff credits: one routine writes the credits text from $FD:A000 ("PRODUCER//KAZUHIKO AOKI"...) one line per frame.
  • A fatal-error stop. One routine blanks the screen to a solid colour, disables interrupts and loops forever. Each of its 13 callers passes its own colour. It came from following up a duplicate.
  • A small quirk in battle. Holding L+R counts frames toward a message ($75). Reviews took three rounds to pin down exactly when that counter resets.

A last batch came from following the duplicate finder's leads into banks $C0, $C2, $CF and $FD: another 1,037 bytes, all reviewed.

Three more batches went in during the afternoon:

  • Battle actions ($C1:4058–$C1:49FE, 2,471 bytes). Service 4 plays one action's script frame by frame, then loads what the action needs: its script, the attack or tech record, graphics sets and the sprite frames. Three bytes at $CF:FFFD-FFFF, all 0 in the shipped game, can force the action flags.
  • What's in front of the leader ($C0, 1,370 bytes). The checks for the object and the tile in front of the party leader, the eight D-pad handlers, and the limits that stop the leader at the edge of a map. The reach test is off by at most one unit, because a missing SEC and a missing INC partly cancel out.
  • Bank $C2 boot (1,229 bytes). The bank's entry points, its interrupt handlers, and the new-game setup that fills in each character's starting record.

Then three more:

  • Map scrolling ($C0, 2,425 bytes). Each of the three background layers keeps its own scroll accumulators in 1/16 pixel; every frame they move one pixel at a time and, when a layer crosses a tile edge, a new row or column of the map is built. Layer 2 has a half-speed mode.
  • Battle action scripts ($C1, 2,231 bytes). Each action runs up to 13 script threads, one opcode at a time. A breadth-first path search finds the way to the target across a grid of occupied cells, giving up after 30 steps.
  • The $C2 scene engine (1,936 bytes). A task system of 64 slots run every frame, a linked list of 64 sprites, the text window, the joypad reader with its soft reset on L+R+Select+Start, and the play-time clock.

And the evening's batches:

  • Map redraws and collision ($C0, 5,951 bytes). The full redraw of each background layer, the row and column writers, and the leader's collision check: each frame's step is tested against walls and other objects, slid around corners, and a blocked diagonal is retried as a straight step. Reviews found five places where the original code adds without clearing the carry first, so a probe lands 1/256 of a tile off; all are documented, none "fixed".
  • Battle action script, opcodes $13-$85 ($C1, 4,267 bytes). Curving moves, path walks, waits and subscripts, script variables, the damage numbers that bounce over battlers, palette flashes and cycles, and sound effects.
  • The $C2 scene loader (2,430 bytes). Each location has a header in bank $C6 naming the packed graphics, palettes, maps and script it needs; the loader unpacks them all and redraws the background from 16x16 metatiles.

Late in the day:

  • Location map setup ($C0, 2,078 bytes). Unpacking a location's map properties, tile planes, exit and treasure tiles (a treasure already taken shows its opened tile), the scroll limits and the scroll origin around the entry point.
  • The $C2 scene script (2,598 bytes). The interpreter for the scripts that drive scene tasks, with 54 of its 83 opcodes, and a second small interpreter for sprite animations.
  • Arc moves and moves along a heading ($C1, 2,485 bytes). Review found that on thread 4 one of them sets every actor's angle and facing but never their "moving" flag, so none of them moves; the header now says so.

main now stands at 71,206 bytes, 19.82% of the game's code, every byte of it independently verified.

In the evening, after a pause for the usage limit:

  • Battle action opcodes $C0-$DA and the opcode table ($C1, 2,704 bytes). Circular and elliptical moves, pointing at a calculated target, counters and attribute bits, and the full 224-entry opcode table with its four loaders. Review caught that the step opcode, which adds in 8 bits until it hits its target, can miss forever: a step of 0, or an even step across an odd gap, never lands on it. The header now says exactly when.
  • The rest of the $C0 location load (2,127 bytes). Tileset, metatile and palette steps, the event data and object init, and the scene reload with its palette and upload helpers.

  • All of the $C2 scene script opcodes (2,606 bytes). The last 29 opcodes, the tile upload task, palette fades, screen fades and mosaic. One opcode that compares a task's age turned out not to stop "for good": the 16-bit frame counter keeps counting while it waits, so it resumes once that counter wraps round to 0.

  • Battle action position calculations ($C1, 2,138 bytes). The 18 ways a battle script picks a point: an entry's position, midpoints, the centroid of a group, a spot ahead of an actor, and smooth moves toward a target, plus the four facing rules. The 963 bytes after them turned out not to be code at all: they are cut-off remains of older, longer builds of the same tables, each shifted by a fixed amount, which a newer, shorter build never overwrote. They are matched as labelled data.

Into the night:

  • Scene layer scrolling, modes and sound zones ($C2, 2,268 bytes). Scenes scroll a layer one pixel at a time and draw each newly visible tile column or row as it comes into view. Modes 2-8 cover a location change, leaving the scene, the menu and the mode-7 sub-program. Sound zones pick the music from a 4-bit map packed at the front of each scene's data. A reviewer found four real calls that the caller tool had dismissed as doubtful, so the tool is on the list for a fix.

  • The battle's main routine ($C1, 2,109 bytes). This one routine runs a whole battle: it shuffles the turn order, counts down 13 per-slot turn lists, checks for victory and defeat, hands out gold and items, and leaves. Next to it are the battle setup and the 16-bit multiply, divide and random-range helpers the rest of the battle uses more than 200 times. A debug "instant win" check reads a flag byte that is 0 in the retail ROM, so it never fires.

  • The field/battle hand-off ($C0, 2,506 bytes). Before a battle the field saves its objects, the party's positions and the PPU settings. Afterwards it rebuilds itself according to the battle's result: wait for a button and restart, reload the location, or rebuild in place. The batch also covers linking objects into and out of their draw lists, the location's audio step, and two tilemap builders. One quirk: a test meant as BIT #$10 reads memory at $0010 instead.

The same batches also tidied 66 older headers that still called now-matched code "unmatched". Each of them went back through review. One turned out to be not just stale but wrong: a hook banner credited code with setting the event hook, when its stores actually land on the map's step counters.

  • Battle turn lists ($C1, 2,065 bytes). The battle keeps 13 per-slot countdown lists. List 12 is the battlers' turns: ready characters get a menu, ready enemies act, queued commands run, and then each enemy's script gets a chance to react. The other lists are status timers: a poison-like hit for a share of max HP, timers that halve or double (probably haste and slow), and plain countdowns that clear a status bit. The 988-byte turn routine needed four review rounds before every claim about its reaction scripts held up against the ROM.

main now stands at 89,729 bytes, 24.97% of the game's code, all 1,026 matched routines independently verified.

Then the workflow got its overhaul. Generated files no longer travel in pull requests, so parallel branches stop conflicting. Callers lines are now written by a tool and left out of the review hash, so matching new code no longer voids older reviews. Three new lint checks catch the header mistakes reviewers kept finding: wrong byte ranges, stale "unmatched" mentions, and Entry lines that leave out DP or DB. The caller-finding tool also learned to follow code through routines that change register widths, which found 39 more real calls in a held-out test.

The first batch through the new pipeline:

  • Scene triggers and the text decoder ($C2, 2,328 bytes). Two watcher state machines for scene objects and tile triggers, and the whole text decoder: its four states and every control code from $00 to $20, covering numbers, character and party-member names, wide glyphs, and tech, enemy and item names. An empty party slot prints the first character's name, because an 8-bit shift drops the "empty" bit. Of 87 routines, 84 passed review the first time, and the lint had already caught four header mistakes before any reviewer saw them.

  • Object motion and view culling ($C0, 2,342 bytes). The per-frame object pass, deciding which objects are in view, stepping objects along straight lines and arcs, and turning an angle into a velocity through the sine table and the hardware multiplier. Also the copy of a map region and the draw pass run at load time. All 21 routines passed review on the first try. The branch also came up to date with a plain merge from main, with no conflicts.

main now stands at 94,399 bytes, 26.27% of the game's code, all 1,130 matched routines independently verified.

Late in the evening, three more batches went through review and merged:

  • The NMI handler and frame wait ($C0, 5,396 bytes). Everything the game does once per frame during vertical blank: palette and sprite uploads, the queued VRAM writes, map redraw steps and the staff-credits line, plus the tiny loop the field spins in until the NMI has done its work. That loop used to be called Sub_EC60. A reviewer pointed out that its header already said exactly what it does, so it is now Field_WaitFrame, and the 15 routines that mention it went back through review. The batch also covers the event commands that walk an object to a tile (they aim for X $80 / Y $F0 inside it: centred, near the bottom), and the sprite tile slots that objects borrow as they come into view. One quirk: an upload address is computed with an ADC that has no CLC before it, so a stray carry adds 1.
  • The party leader and followers ($C2, 5,182 bytes). In the $C2 scenes, the leader walks in 8-pixel steps and scrolls the background as it goes. Its buttons switch scene modes, and it idles, animates, and walks onto objects. The other members follow it with their own small route planner, which scans rows and columns of the scene map for a way round obstacles. The batch also covers the glyph drawing behind the text decoder: 2bpp and 4bpp blitters, the width tables and the number formatting.
  • Enemy behaviour scripts ($C1, 2,415 bytes). The core that reads each enemy's script: a list of blocks, each one or two tests followed by actions, plus a separate reaction part. A block whose tests hold chooses its next action, and later turns step through the block's actions in order. Two finds: one action code jumps back into the middle of the test-passed routine after picking a random action (25/50/75% thresholds for one, two or three steps further along), and one target picker loops forever if an enemy's target marks disagree. The routine that turns a hit into a record offset also wraps for the last two slots of the sixth hit set. Thirty of its 39 routines passed review the first time; the other nine needed a second round, and one a third.

main now stands at 107,392 bytes, 29.89% of the game's code, all 1,373 matched routines independently verified.

Around midnight, four more batches went through review and merged:

  • Player commands ($C1, 5,174 bytes). What happens after a party member picks a command: the battler checks each pass makes (the low-HP pose bit, which turn lists a battler takes part in, the KO check), the command runner for attacks, techs and items, the tech MP costs and who pays them, and the end-of-battle copies back to the field. The batch was written before the workflow overhaul, so it was ported onto the new layout first. Review found that a tech's first user never gets its extra wait: the divisor is never stored, so the code divides by 0, which the divide routine answers with 0. A KO'd party member with the right flag is revived with a heal that is recorded twice, once as a positive amount for the action and once negated for the hit set.
  • Battle helpers in bank $FD (5,364 bytes). The enemy rewards, the battle item list, restoring enemies, stat boosts from equipment, the first gauge values and the turn-list timers, plus the field's HDMA set-up and location animation loaders. One routine builds a brightness gradient for the screen as 90 pairs of colour-math bytes. Merging it with the player-command batch turned up 18 names defined twice, which the assembler accepts silently, so each now has one definition.
  • Field event commands ($C0, 5,016 bytes). Dozens of event-script opcodes: calls into other objects' scripts, jumps and conditions, button tests, loads, stores and block copies, arithmetic and bit operations, animation and wait commands, and the message commands. The message commands halt the game with a coloured screen if no message pointer was set.
  • Scene objects ($C2, 5,272 bytes). Two objects in the $C2 scenes that the party can get into (probably vehicles), their position markers, two companions that glide after object B, and a task that draws a label (probably a place name) as a sprite above the party. One of them reads absolute address $0028 instead of its own facing byte.

main now stands at 128,218 bytes, 35.69% of the game's code, all 1,715 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Matching continues with the rest of the field event commands in $C0, the mode 6 and mode 8 sub-programs in $C2, and the item and tech handling in $C1. The wiki pages are also being brought up to date one by one.

docs.title: 9 October 2026: event commands, battle effects, the dial and the menu threads
docs.text: Two more batches went through review overnight: the second half of the field's event-script commands in $C0, and the part of the battle engine that resolves an action's targets and runs its effects in $C1. Together 10,245 bytes in 143 routines, all independently verified.

docs.title: Event commands, part two
docs.text:
The field's event scripts drive almost everything that happens outside battle. This batch ($C0, 5,214 bytes) covers the commands that move the party, give and take items and gold, add and remove party members, warp to other locations, play music and sound effects, fade the screen, shake it, and set up characters and sprites. The credits use a few of them too.

Two finds along the way:

  • A block of RAM the code had called Map_Unk7F3700 turned out to hold small event scripts: one walks a party member back to the leader, three walk a member to a tile and turn it, and one remembers a script position.
  • Several commands hand work to the menu code in bank $C2, and their headers first claimed the Y register came back unchanged. It does not: the menu side never saves it, and a later restore even clears its high byte. Review caught this in twelve headers.

docs.title: Targets and effects
docs.text:
When a tech or an item is used, the battle engine first works out who it hits, then runs its effects one part at a time. This batch ($C1, 5,031 bytes) covers the target resolution, the runner that steps through a tech's parts, the MP check, the first effect types and the table that dispatches them, and a set of fixed-fraction scaling helpers. Five of the eight scalers have no caller at all.

Review found two quirks worth keeping:

  • Two scratch variables in the target routine overlap, so a second entry in an area record would be read from the wrong place. No area record in the game has a second entry, so it never matters.
  • On one path the final store reads entry $FF of the target list, well past its end, because a counter is 0 when 1 is subtracted from it.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text:
• CI now really checks the ROM's hash. Before, it looked for a file that does not exist in the repository and quietly skipped the check.
  • The function notes in the symbol list now start at the beginning of a sentence instead of halfway through.
  • The caller-finding tool's tests were pinned to code that has since been matched. They now test the same thing without depending on how much is matched.
  • Every page of this wiki was checked against the current source and brought up to date, and five new system pages describe the frame cycle, the field event scripts, the scene engine, the text windows and battle actions.

docs.title: The map view and the dial
docs.text:
A third batch ($C2, 4,850 bytes) followed in the early hours: two of the $C2 scenes' special modes and the menu's own interrupt handler.

  • The map view (mode 6) builds a Mode 7 picture of the whole scene, one pixel across and two down per map tile, zooms out from the leader, shows position markers over a blue gradient and zooms back in on a button press.
  • The dial (mode 8) lets the player turn a hand to one of seven location markers. The hand is a triangle drawn line by line into the window registers' HDMA tables, and the pick becomes object A's next destination, which settles a question the scene-object batch had left open.

Most of review's findings were one recurring slip: headers saying a routine takes either X width when it really needs 16-bit X. All 20 were fixed and passed a second review.

main now stands at 143,313 bytes, 39.89% of the game's code, all 1,933 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: The effect arithmetic
docs.text:
Next came the arithmetic behind the battle effects in $C1 (4,347 bytes): restoring HP and MP, curing and setting status, the hit roll, damage and its formulas, the hit, evade and defence adjustments, the timed-status lists, drain, steal, and the bank's small service table for finding, adding and removing items and gold.

The code has some real bugs, all kept as found and documented:

  • Damage kinds 8 to 10 never work as intended, because one test is inverted.
  • One effect can never miss: its miss flag is stored to the wrong byte.
  • Two of the timed-status lists are never started; the code that would start them cannot be reached.
  • Adding an item to a full inventory overwrites the first slot.
  • Gold is capped at 9,999,999, but adding to a total of 9,961,472 or more can lose money instead when the low part overflows: 9,999,999 + 30,000 leaves 9,964,463.

Review sent six headers back, mostly for wording that was close but not exact about edge cases. All six were fixed and passed a second review.

docs.title: The last event commands
docs.text:
The final batch of event-script commands in $C0 (5,611 bytes) completed the field's command table: the remaining handlers, the 256-entry table itself (32 of its entries are never used), the party's walking and running animations with their 65-entry table, the message window, the animated map tiles, and the field's interrupt handler, which uploads one tile-animation job each time it runs. A routine that had been called an audio sync turned out to touch no sound at all; it refreshes the HDMA tables and is now named for that.

Four headers needed fixes, among them an address range that stopped two bytes short and a register claimed to be "any" when a callee needs it zero. All four passed a second review.

main now stands at 153,271 bytes, 42.66% of the game's code, all 2,022 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: The menu's threads and the scene effects
docs.text:
The last batch of the day was the biggest in $C2 so far (5,349 bytes, 540 of them empty $FF fill at the end of the scene code). It covers the scene engine's screen effects (BG3 drifts, waves and slides, window effects, a noise effect, BG2 line waves, saving and restoring the party), the menu's entry point, and the machinery the rest of the menu runs on.

The menu is built from cooperative threads. A scheduler runs up to eight of them, each with its own 64-byte stack. A thread runs until it calls a yield routine, which saves its registers on its own stack and hands over to the next one; it carries on from the same spot a frame (or a set number of frames) later. The cursors, the scrolling-list arrows and the fades are each a thread. One detail the review caught: the scheduler never resets the data bank between threads, so each thread starts with whatever bank the previous one left.

Quirks kept as found include a block copy that writes one byte past the end of its buffer, a cursor drawn one pixel low because a helper is called in the wrong register width, and a list arrow that can sit nine pixels lower instead of eight.

Review found 22 header errors, most of them about what a register holds on exit. The most common: an instruction that switches the index registers to 8 bits wipes their high bytes for good, so a header cannot say Y comes back unchanged after calling such a routine. The same slip turned up in three older menu routines, which were fixed too. It took three rounds, but every routine in the batch is now independently verified.

main now stands at 158,620 bytes, 44.15% of the game's code, all 2,135 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: Hit modifiers, experience and tech points
docs.text:
Back in $C1 (3,521 bytes), the 21 small handlers that the damage routine runs after working out a hit turned out to be hit modifiers: most scale the damage, some set a status, change HP or leave the target on 1 HP. The same batch covers what happens after a battle: experience and level-ups with their HP and MP growth, tech points, and learning single and combo techs. One quirk, kept as found: when one award of tech points pays for a tech and reaches into the next, part of it is taken off the next tech's cost a second time. Reserve characters gain at most one level per battle.

Review again turned up the Y register slip (the random number routine switches the index registers to 8 bits, so nothing that rolls a random number can return Y unchanged), and two more older routines with the same error were fixed with the batch.

docs.title: Bank $C0 is complete
docs.text: The last 3,234 bytes of $C0 are matched, so every byte of the bank now comes from source. They hold a routine run from the field's interrupt that draws what is probably the cursor of a message choice, 400 bytes of cut-off code left over from older builds, and four lookup tables: an angle table, a direction-to-facing table and two sine tables, each checked against its formula entry by entry.

docs.title: Counting code and data separately
docs.text: With $C0 complete, the progress figure showed it as 106% matched, because the share counted every matched byte, tables and padding included, against a survey of code bytes only. The progress tool now tells code and data apart and measures the share with code alone; data is reported next to it. The survey for $C0 also turned out 922 bytes too high. The headline figure is therefore lower than this post's earlier sections give: by the new measure, main now stands at 154,931 of 358,356 code bytes, 43.23%, plus 10,444 bytes of data, all 2,184 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: Catching one kind of mistake for good
docs.text: One slip kept coming back in review: a header saying a routine leaves the Y register unchanged, when somewhere along the way (often in a routine it calls) the index registers are switched to 8 bits, which wipes Y's high byte for good. A sweep of all 618 such claims in the source found 23 that were wrong, all fixed and re-reviewed. The lint now checks every claim of this kind itself, following each path through the routine and the routines it calls, so a wrong one cannot get past the checks again. On its first run against the open batches it caught one more.

docs.title: Enemy behaviour scripts
docs.text: Enemies decide what to do with small scripts: a list of tests ("is my HP at most half?", "is a party member in the same row?", a random chance) followed by what to choose and what to run. The handlers for all three are now matched in $C1 (5,451 bytes): 34 tests, the choose handlers, and 23 actions, from attacking and using a tech to swapping in a waiting enemy, leaving the battle or changing the enemy's own stats. Many of the values they read are still unnamed, so most names are careful guesses, marked as such. A few are real bugs, kept as found: one test reads the knock-out flag from the wrong byte, and two actions skip a check and read from the wrong address when no helper is present.

docs.title: The message window's frame and the palette animator
docs.text:
In $FD (5,805 bytes), the routines that build the field's per-line display tables are matched. They draw a band across the screen that opens line by line from the middle of a fixed position, near the top or the bottom depending on where the speaker stands, and it turned out to be the message window: the field's message code opens it by up to four lines a frame, to 40, and closes it again. The other half is the palette animator that runs every frame, copying, rotating, pulsing and fading colours, with a quirk where a pulse goes black for one frame where full brightness was meant.

main now stands at 166,187 of 358,356 code bytes, 46.37%, plus 10,444 bytes of data, all 2,290 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: The menu's commands and the main menu
docs.text:
The last batch of the day ($C2, about 5,000 bytes) fills in most of what the menu does before any screen opens: the command dispatcher the field and battle code call to change the party, refill records, check the save slots at boot and equip items; every setup routine the menu runs when it starts (graphics, OAM, the item tables, the window graphics and palette); the recalculation of a character's stats from their equipment; the save-slot summaries and labels; the menu's animated character sprites; and the main menu itself. The handlers of the other menu modes are next.

Two quirks worth knowing: the routine that multiplies by 64 only keeps A intact when called with a 16-bit accumulator, and one save-slot summary writes three flag bytes over the start of data it has just copied.

main now stands at 170,895 of 358,356 code bytes, 47.69%, plus 10,748 bytes of data, all 2,403 matched routines independently verified.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Matching continues with the menu's mode handlers in $C2, the enemy scripts' target handlers in $C1 and the rest of the palette animator in $FD, while a survey maps the banks no one has started yet.

docs.title: Progress summary
docs.text: Bank What is matched there $C0 The field engine: game loop, frame wait and NMI handler, location loading, map scrolling, object motion, the event script opcodes, the sprite system, and the reset code, header and vectors at the top of the bank $C1 The battle engine: BattleSys_Main and its turn lists, the enemy behaviour scripts, the PC command runner, action scripts, the battle menu, targeting and status bar $C2 The scene mode (tasks, scripts, sprite list, scene loading) and the text window decoder $FD MainInit, the battle helpers bank $C1 calls with JSL, the field HDMA set-up and the location animation set-up $CC, $CF, $FF Copies of matched code kept in other banks: the 8×8 multiply ($CC), a scaled sine and a four-digit number formatter ($CF), the wave tables ($FF)

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
One page per game system: a summary written by hand from the matched code's headers, then, on the pages that have one, the routines that belong to it, generated from functions.csv in the code repo. A routine's group is the subsystem column there, taken from its name's prefix; "Engine (unnamed)" holds matched engine routines that still carry Sub_ labels. The table below counts every group.

Page Covers Boot Vectors, reset, MainInit, the cold init Frame cycle and NMI One field frame, the frame wait, NmiHandler, the field IRQ, the other modes' frames Engine core The field: game loop, location loading, the map, scene changes, objects Field event scripts The objects' byte-code scripts and their opcodes Sprites & objects Animation, frame builds, the OAM shadow Scene engine Bank $C2's scene mode: tasks, scripts, sprite list, scene loading, the map view and the dial Text windows Bank $C2's text decoder Menu Bank $C2's menu: entry, thread scheduler, interrupts, shared helpers Battle engine BattleSys_Main, turn lists, enemy behaviour scripts, PC commands, effects and damage, hit records, bank $FD helpers Battle actions Service 4, the action scripts and the enemy movers Battle menu The command menu, its lists and input Battle targeting Target modes and area shapes Status bar & text The battle status bar and number formatting

Field event scripts, frame cycle, scene engine, text windows, the menu and battle actions are parts of the larger "Engine" and "Battle engine" groups, so their routines are listed on the Engine core and Battle engine pages.

To add a system: give its routines a subsystem in the code repo (a name prefix in tools/progress.py), add a page here (copy any existing one and change its wk:system marker), add it to the nav in mkdocs.yml, and run tools/sync_progress.py.
