docs.title: Battle actions
docs.text:
How the battle plays one action, an attack, a tech or the like: service 4 of bank $C1's service dispatcher loads the action's script, graphics and palette steps, then runs the script frame by frame until it ends. The whole of this machinery, $C1:4058–$C1:7C3C, is matched: the service, its loaders, the reach check and path search, the thread runner and every opcode handler. "Action", "attack" and "tech" are the headers' readings of the records the loaders take; they are not checked against what the player sees.

These routines belong to the "Battle engine" group, so their table is on the Battle engine page.

See also: Battle engine, Battle targeting.

docs.title: Service 4: BattleSys_RunAction
docs.text:
BattleSys_RunAction ($C1:4058, 358 bytes) is reached only through the dispatcher (entry 4 of the table at $C1:0051). The one request found is BattleSys_UnkBFA4, called only by BattleSys_UnkAC57, which then applies the hits (Battle_ApplyHits); BattleSys_UnkAC57 is called by the enemy turn (BattleAi_EnemyTurn), the PC command runner (BattleSys_UnkB967, BattleSys_RunPcAttack), the KO check and a turn-list helper. It plays the action described by the block at Battle_ActCaster (caster, kind, id, target masks), filled from the chosen command (for an enemy by BattleAi_FillActBlock):

  1. reset the action state and wait a frame;
  2. build the battler lists (BattleAct_BuildBattlerList) and load the script (BattleAct_LoadScript);
  3. each frame: the battlers' action animations (BattleAct_StepBattlerAnims, at most one frame decoded per frame), the menu, palette steps, the per-entry calculations (BattleAct_TickCalcs), the occupied-cell map, the probes, and the script threads (BattleAct_RunThreads), until the script says it has ended;
  4. send APU command $18, wait until Battle_Unk5D9B is 0, and pick every battler's status animation again (Battle_PickNextStatusAnim);
  5. if a PC was among the targets, flag each PC whose pending hit reaches its HP (BattleAct_FlagLethalPcHits) and draw that PC's KO frame.

docs.title: Loading an action
docs.text:
BattleAct_LoadScript ($C1:4310) clears the 16-byte parameter block and calls one loader per Battle_ActKind through BattleAct_LoaderTable ($C1:7A63):

Kind Loader Reads 0 (and 4 up) BattleAct_LoadNone nothing; no thread starts 1 BattleAct_LoadAttack ($C1:432C) three record sets per PC, two records per enemy type (the "attack" reading is a guess) 2 BattleAct_LoadTech ($C1:45A0) a 7-byte record per action id, for PCs and enemies (the "tech" reading is a guess) 3 BattleAct_LoadKind3 ($C1:475B) like the PC tech branch, for any caster, with id − $BC

Each record gives a script number, two graphics sets, and indexes of the compressed sprite frames, the palette steps and the object lists. All loaders end in BattleAct_LoadCommon, which loads the graphics sets, unpacks the sprite frames into $7E:2D00 (BattleAct_UnpackFrames, through the $C3:0002 vector) and splits the object records (BattleAct_IndexObjLists). The PC command runner uses kind 3 for items (id = item id); whether BattleAct_LoadKind3 is "the item loader" is still open in NEXT.md.

Before a PC's attack is loaded, BattleAct_CheckReach decides whether the target is near enough, and BattleAct_FindPath ($C1:4A71) is a breadth-first search on the path map from the attacker's cell to the target's.

docs.title: Script threads
docs.text:
A script starts with two 16-bit thread masks (bit 15 down to bit 0 for threads 0–15), then one offset per set bit. Every frame BattleAct_RunThreads ($C1:4BBE) runs one step of each live thread, in the order 0–4, then 8–15. A thread stands for an actor:

Threads Actor 0–3 The battler in that entry of Battle_ActBattlers: the caster, the two partner slots, the main target 4 Every slot of the target set, while the target mask is non-zero 5–7 Never run 8–15 Object threads 0–7, which drive the action's own objects

BattleAct_RunThread ($C1:4C9E) runs opcodes through BattleAct_OpcodeTable ($C1:7A6B, 224 words) until a handler stops it for the frame. Only opcodes below $DB run, so the last five entries are never reached; 75 entries point at BattleAct_OpEndScript (opcode $01 and the unused opcodes), and there are 115 distinct handlers. A handler moves the script on with BattleAct_AdvanceScript; one that does not (a wait) runs again next frame.

The opcode handlers ($C1:4CF0–$C1:75BA) fall into groups, each with its own banner:

  • Control: end the thread or script, call and return, pause, the waits on script variables, follow / unfollow.
  • Animation: play, loop or show an animation frame of the actor, set its speed and facing.
  • Movement: straight moves (BattleAct_OpMoveTo), curving moves, path walks (BattleAct_OpPathTo, using BattleAct_FindPath), arcs (BattleAct_OpArcToCalc), circles and ellipses, moves along a heading, the midpoint move, the shake (BattleAct_OpShake), and the position history.
  • Script variables: set, count, add, copy and swap them.
  • Hit numbers: BattleAct_OpShowHitNumbers ($C1:5ADB).
  • Palettes: load an entry, start and stop palette sequences, a special palette and its restore, colour rotation and blinking.
  • Sound: APU commands $18/$19 with an id (BattleAct_OpSound), and the PC attack sounds.

Many opcodes take a point from one of two dispatchers: BattleAct_CalcFacing (25 facing modes: like an entry, toward an entry, fixed, toward the centre) and BattleAct_RunCalc (72 point calculations: a battler's position, a midpoint, a centroid, a fixed point, a saved position, an object's offset, a point along a line). Their tables are BattleAct_FacingModeTable and BattleAct_CalcTable ($C1:79A1–$C1:7A62).

docs.title: Enemy movers
docs.text: Outside actions, enemies move by themselves in 8-pixel steps ($C1:3714–$C1:4057): Battle_TickEnemyMovers runs, each frame, the mover picked by the enemy's animation through Battle_EnemyMoverTable (9 entries): stay put, approach the target, charge, line up on one axis, keep to a ring round the target, orbit it, loop round an ellipse, fixed directions, head for the screen centre. Each picks the heading of the next step and tests the box there against the cell map and the other battlers; the stepper that then moves the enemy ($CF:F978) is not matched.

docs.title: Not matched yet
docs.text:
From NEXT.md: the movers in bank $CF that the movement opcodes hand over to (dispatch at $CF:EFC4), the position-history recorder $CF:ED1D, the hit-number bounce $CF:E781, the colour rotation $CF:E600, the palette stepper BattleAct_StepPalettes and the action helpers in bank $CC. NEXT.md also still lists as open "the code at $C1:ACF0 that fills the action block"; those bytes now lie inside matched routines (BattleAi_ArgToDp0E ends at $C1:ACF1, BattleAi_FillActBlock starts at $C1:ACF2).

The banner before BattleSys_RunAction still says the script interpreter "is not matched yet", and the thread banner calls BattleAct_OpcodeTable unmatched; both are now matched (the second is listed in NEXT.md as stale).

docs.title: Battle engine
docs.text:
Bank $C1 is the battle engine; nearly all of it is one system. The battle runs with DP=$0000 and DB=$7E, and keeps its state in bank-$7E WRAM (names in asm/include/ram_battle.inc, all starting with Battle, Battler, Pc, Enemy, Tech, Item or Sfx). Long helpers in bank $FD (BattleFD_*) do much of its setup and its ends.

This page covers the battle's structure and the shared services. The parts with their own pages: Battle actions (service 4 and the action scripts), Battle menu, Battle targeting and Status bar & text.

"Victory", "defeat", "attack", "tech", "item" and the like below follow the headers, which take them from the services' and records' known roles; where a header hedges, so does this page.

docs.title: Entering and leaving
docs.text: The field enters the battle with JSL $C10000 (in DefaultHandler, $C0:18A7). Per the headers that chain runs JMP $001B → JML $CF:FB65 (which clears the battle RAM) → $C1:8000 (BankC1_BattleStartVec) → BattleSys_Main. The battle leaves through BattleSys_ExitVec ($C1:0006 → $001F → JML $CF:FBE5); the vectors at $C1:0000–$0050 and the code in bank $CF are not matched yet. On the field side Scene_Unk0283 reads FieldBtl_Result to decide how to come back.

docs.title: BattleSys_Main
docs.text:
BattleSys_Main ($C1:8006, 1,115 bytes) is the battle from its setup to its end; it never returns.

Setup. BattleFD_UnkA982, the random index, Battle_SetupBattle ($C1:FA8B: the battlers' records, the enemies' stats, the PCs' tech menus, the turn-list state, mostly through bank-$FD callees), then service 0. Then two shuffles with Battle_RandRange: Battle_SlotOrder, a random order of the battlers taking part, and Battle_EnemyOrder, the present enemies in a random order. Then BattleSys_Unk8C09, which runs the main part of each enemy's behaviour script once.

Each pass of the main loop: service 3 (BattleSys_UpkeepTwoFrames, two frames of upkeep), the KO checks (BattleSys_UnkB223), then the first of:

  • Battle_Unk24 set: the defeat end;
  • no enemy entry left: the victory end;
  • otherwise the low-HP bits and the turn-list membership of every battler (BattleSys_UnkB093, BattleSys_UnkB0B6), then by state: in wait mode (Battle_MenuTimeHold) only the PCs' pending commands; with Battle_Unk99CD set its end (probably running away; not traced); with Battle_UnkAF25 set the turn handler BattleSys_Unk8461 directly; else the turn lists.

Ends. Victory plays service 8 (BattleSys_VictoryPose), puts the max HP back and adds the gold and item rewards, then hands out the experience and tech points (BattleSys_AwardExpAndTp, see After a won battle); defeat runs service 3 eight times and then service 9 (BattleSys_DefeatPose). A dead debug check (.debug_check, pad 2) can end the battle as a win. The defeat, victory and Battle_Unk99CD ends clear the PCs' battle statuses (BattleSys_ClearPcStatuses: .Status2 and the eight .Unk4C bytes, everything in .Status but the KO bit; "so the battle statuses do not outlast it, probably"), and BattleSys_ClearPcKo then clears .Status altogether, KO bit included (after the victory messages, and on the end shared by defeat, the Battle_Unk99CD end and the bit-5 battle). All ends save the random index back and copy Battle_Unk1C48 entries to the PCs' BattlerStats.Unk56 before BattleFD_UnkAAB0.

docs.title: Turn lists
docs.text:
Thirteen per-slot lists ($C1:8461–$C1:8C3D), each one byte per list and battler slot in four 13 × 11-byte arrays: Battle_ListTimers (countdowns), Battle_ListFlags (bit 7 due, low bits "takes part"), Battle_ListRuns (runs left) and Battle_ListReload (timer reload). BattleSys_Main counts the timers down each pass; every second pass it scans each list for the next due slot in Battle_SlotOrder and runs that list's entry of BattleSys_ListHandlerTable ($C1:B92D).

List Handler What it does 0, 2–5, 10 BattleSys_ListHandler0 … The usual handler: re-arm the entry, count its runs down, and at 0 clear one status bit of the slot and stop the entry 1 BattleSys_ListHandler1 A repeating hit on the slot (inferred from where the amount goes) 6, 7, 11 BattleSys_ListHandler6/7/11 Nothing (RTS) 8, 9 BattleSys_ListHandler8/9 Re-arm with the timer halved or doubled by status bits 12 BattleSys_Unk8461 The battlers' turns: a ready PC is queued for the command menu (service 1), a ready enemy acts (BattleAi_EnemyTurn), committed PC commands run (BattleSys_UnkB967), then the enemies' reaction scripts

The banner reads lists 0–5 and 8–10 as timed statuses from their shape; which status each list is, is not traced.

docs.title: Enemy behaviour scripts
docs.text:
An enemy's script lives in bank $CC at the address !BattleRom_AiScriptPtrs gives for its id. It has two parts, each ended by $FF: the main part, run for each enemy by BattleSys_Unk8C09 / BattleAi_RunMainPart ($C1:AFD2), and the reaction part, run by BattleSys_Unk8461 after a turn (BattleAi_FindReactPart, $C1:B488). A part is a list of blocks; a block is one or two 4-byte test records ending in $FE, then action records ending in $FE. The first byte of a record is its code:

Table Address Entries Run by BattleAi_TestTable $C1:B80D 41 test codes $00–$28 BattleAi_RunMainPart, the reaction loop BattleAi_ChooseTable $C1:B85F 23 action codes $00–$16 BattleAi_TestPassed, as a block is chosen BattleAi_RunTable $C1:B88D the same 23 action codes BattleAi_EnemyTurn, on the enemy's turn BattleAi_TargetTable $C1:B8BB 57 target codes $00–$38 BattleAi_ReadTargets

A test that holds calls BattleAi_TestPassed ($C1:8C3E), which runs the block's next action through the choose table; on the enemy's turn BattleAi_EnemyTurn ($C1:8CF9) runs it again through the run table; the action block that service 4 plays is started by BattleAi_FillActBlock. Target codes fill the list BattleAi_Targets, with helpers that pick PCs by a stat-block byte, cut the list down to one, or keep the marked entries ($C1:AC14–$C1:AF21). The names "test", "action" and "target" are inferred from what the matched handlers do. The handlers themselves (BattleAi_TestNN etc., $C1:8EAB–$C1:AC13) are not matched yet, except test $00, which always holds.

docs.title: PC commands and techs
docs.text:
BattleSys_UnkB967 ($C1:B967, the "PC command runner") runs the command a PC committed in the battle menu, from its BattleCmd record: an attack through BattleSys_RunPcAttack, an item as action kind 3, or a tech as kind 2 with its users' MP paid (BattleSys_PayTechMp); then it reloads the users' gauges (!Battler_UnkAFAB, probably the ATB gauge's reload value) and clears the records (BattleSys_UnkBCE1, BattleSys_ResetTechUsers).

Battle_SetupBattle builds each PC's 20 tech menu entries with BattleSys_UnkC96A, BattleSys_UnkCA1A and BattleSys_UnkCCCB ($C1:C96A–$C1:CDFE): single techs at entries 0–7, up to 6 double techs at 10–15 and a triple tech at 18, each only when all its users are in the party. A tech's record names its users and each user's part; BattleSys_TechMpCost1-3 read each part's MP cost and BattleSys_AdjustMpCost halves or quarters it by a per-PC byte.

Before a command runs, BattleSys_UnkC1DD ($C1:C1DD–$C1:C8F6) checks that the caster and its partners can act (not KO'd, no status that stops them) and resolves the targets into a list of slots from the tech's, item's or enemy action's target mode and area number; if that fails the action is dropped.

docs.title: Effects and damage
docs.text:
A tech (or a PC's attack) runs as up to three parts, one per user. BattleSys_RunTechParts ($C1:D523) checks the MP, then for each part copies a 12-byte effect record whose byte 0, the effect type, picks a routine from BattleSys_EffectTable ($C1:D9D7, 45 words; types $09–$28 do nothing). An item runs one of types $29–$2B straight from BattleSys_UnkBF46, and the enemy runners BattleSys_UnkD7C4 / D8D1 use the same table. The effect routines ($C1:D221–$C1:D48E) work on the targets from the last to the first. Their headers read them, "probably", as: 0 restores HP / MP, 1 cures statuses, 2 sets statuses, 3 is a hit with damage, 5 drains HP / MP, 6 steals, 7 gives up the caster's HP, 8 repeats type 3.

The arithmetic they call ($C1:DA37–$C1:E89E, and BattleSys_StealItem at $C1:E9D5):

  • Restore (BattleSys_RestoreHpMp): HP by an amount × a factor plus a random part (for a PC capped at 999), or the full maximum for factor $0F; MP the same way, in tens.
  • Statuses: BattleSys_CureStatus clears them (KO too, with a flag) and the PC's turn-list flags; BattleSys_SetStatus sets status bits in one of six status bytes (for the first three, only when the target lacks those bits in a byte the header reads as "probably the target's protection"), and BattleSys_ArmStatusList starts the turn list that times the new status (lists 0, 3, 4 and 5 clear their bit when they run out).
  • Type 3, a hit: an enemy-only bit test ("probably an immunity"), then the hit roll (BattleSys_RollHit: chance = caster's value × 100 / target's value against a roll of 0–99, the two values first adjusted by statuses in BattleSys_AdjustHit / BattleSys_AdjustEvade), then the damage. BattleSys_CalcDamage picks a formula by an effect byte (kinds 1–7), each a mix of the caster's stats scaled by another effect byte, with a random part bounded by one of the fixed fractions (Battle_Scale*, $C1:C02A–$C1:C1DC: about x / 5, x × 3 / 10 and so on, built from shifts and subtractions); the caster's status bits then raise or cut the amount. BattleSys_AdjustDefence gives a defence out of 256 from an effect byte or the target's stats, cut by its statuses, and BattleSys_ApplyDamage takes (256 − defence) / 256 of the damage plus the random part, at least 1, runs the hit modifiers on it, then cuts it to 7/10 for two statuses (probably barriers) unless the effect pierces them, and caps it at 9999. A hit also clears two status bits that BattleSys_WakeTarget reads as a status a hit ends ("sleep, probably").
  • Drain (BattleSys_DrainHpMp, type 5): a share of the target's maximum HP or MP plus a random part, capped at what it has, taken from the target and given to the caster.
  • Steal (BattleSys_StealItem, type 6, or type 3 with an effect bit): "an item taken from the target enemy, probably". A roll of 0–99 against a chance from the effect record (tripled for one caster value); on success it runs the part's hit modifier, and one of the enemy's two reward items goes to the caster's item record or the inventory (the second item first when modifier $0C said so). Each of the two can be taken once.

docs.title: Hit modifiers
docs.text:
The 21 routines BattleSys_HitMod* ($C1:ED89–$C1:F204) are picked through BattleSys_HitModTable ($C1:FA61, 21 words) by byte 0 of a 3-byte record in the ROM table !BattleRom_UnkCC2A05; bytes 1 and 2 are their two arguments. BattleSys_RunUnkB2CCHandler ($C1:EB1C) runs one record; BattleSys_RunUnkB2CCHandlers ($C1:EA6F) runs the action part's record and then, when effect byte 8 has bit 7 and the caster's .Unk74 bit 0 is set, the caster's own record (.Unk73). BattleSys_ApplyDamage runs them after it has worked out the damage and before the barrier cuts and the 9999 cap, so most of them change that amount; BattleSys_StealItem runs one too. Which techs or weapons use which record is not traced. "A roll" here is 0–99, and most chances pass at roll ≤ the argument.

Modifier Routine What it does $00 BattleSys_HitModChanceMul On a roll (from the second random index, Battle_RandRangeAlt) at most the caster's .Unk72, multiplies the damage and sets a flag for $13; "together these look like a critical hit (probably ...), not proven" $01 BattleSys_HitModNone Nothing $02 BattleSys_HitModScale Damage × argument 1 / argument 2 $03 BattleSys_HitModUnk47Scale When the target's .Unk47 has one of the given bits, damage × argument 2 / 2 $04 BattleSys_HitModPerEmptyPc Damage × (1 + the number of empty PC slots) $05 BattleSys_HitModPlayTime A factor picked by the play-time clock (its second byte mod 10): about / 10, halved, unchanged, see the quirk, doubled or tripled $06 BattleSys_HitModRandomStatus Sets one of four .Status2 bits, picked by a roll $07, $08 BattleSys_HitModUnk47Status, HitModChanceStatus On a roll, sets the given .Status2 bits ($07 only when the target's .Unk47 has one of the given bits, and on a fixed roll ≤ 80) $09 BattleSys_HitModLeaveOneHp On a roll, the hit leaves the target 1 HP $0A BattleSys_HitModUnk6CScale Scales the damage by one of four target bytes (.Unk6C–.Unk6F, 4 being normal) picked by the action's bits; a byte's bit 7 turns the hit into healing. "This looks like four resistances by element (probably), not proven" $0B BattleSys_HitModScaleThenUnk6C $02, then $0A $0C BattleSys_HitModRollDp1A For the steal: on a roll below argument 1, try the enemy's second item first $0D BattleSys_HitModRestore By argument 1's bits: a full HP restore of the target ("probably"), and/or its statuses cleared $0E BattleSys_HitModHalveHp Unless the target's .Unk46 bit 7 is set, on a roll the damage is half its current HP $0F, $14 BattleSys_HitModClearBits, HitModSetBits Clear or set the given bits in the target's byte at BattlerStats.Unk2D + argument 1 $10 BattleSys_HitModHpDigit Damage × the last decimal digit of the caster's HP / argument 2 $11 BattleSys_HitModZeroHp Sets the caster's HP to 0 ("probably an attack that costs the user its life") or the target's $12 BattleSys_HitModKoOrDrop Unless the target's .Unk46 bit 7 is set, on a roll its HP goes to 0; otherwise the target is dropped from the action $13 BattleSys_HitModAltBoost After a $00 success: damage 9999, or doubled

Quirks the headers keep: for factors 5–6, HitModPlayTime adds half of the word at $0000 (whatever the caller left there) where "x 1.5" looks intended; HitModZeroHp does not check the slot, so for a PC target its KO mark lands in the three bytes below the enemy array.

Two routines in this stretch are never called: BattleSys_AddBattleItem ($C1:EFD3, one more of an item in the battle's item list, else the inventory) and BattleSys_ReviveHeal ($C1:EB49, which looks like "probably an older form" of BattleSys_UpdateKo's one-time revive).

The headers keep the quirks found here, among them BattleSys_CalcDamage's test for kind 8, which branches the wrong way so that its block runs for every kind but 1–8 and the code for kinds 9 and 10 is never reached.

docs.title: Hit records
docs.text: Amounts to take off HP or MP are 4-byte entries per battler slot, in sets of 11 ($C1:E89F–$C1:E8BF, $C1:EBF8–$C1:ED88): Battle_RecordHit stores one (negated, it heals), Battle_ClearCancelledHits drops the cancelled ones, and Battle_ApplyHits ($C1:EC7F) takes them off CurHp / CurMp, clamps to the maximum, and KOs a battler whose HP reaches 0 (an enemy adds its rewards first, BattleFD_AddEnemyRewards).

docs.title: After a won battle
docs.text:
BattleSys_AwardExpAndTp ($C1:F93E) hands out two sums over the defeated enemies' reward records: Battle_UnkB28C and Battle_UnkB2DB. The headers read them as experience and tech points from what the code does with them: the first is added to a 24-bit total and, against a table of experience to the next level, raises PcStatBlk.Level; the second is paid against tech costs and sets the bits the tech menus read. The routines ($C1:F205–$C1:FA60) set the bits that BattleFD_UnkAD17 shows its end messages by.

  • Experience. For each PC in the battle that is not KO'd, BattleSys_AddExp adds the whole sum to .Exp (capped at 9,999,999), then BattleSys_LevelUpStep runs until the sum is used up: BattleSys_ApplyExpStep pays .ExpNeed from it and, when it covers the need, raises the level (to at most 99) and loads the next need. A level-up adds HP and MP from per-character growth rows (BattleSys_GrowHpMp, capped at 999 and 99) and recomputes six stats as a base plus a growth byte × (level − 1) / 100; the stat bytes are then capped at 99, one of them at 50.
  • Characters not in the battle (BattleSys_AwardReserveExp): each character whose bit is set in Menu_Unk29AF and who has no battle slot gets the sum × 15 / 20 and one level step.
  • Tech points. BattleSys_AwardTechPoints pays the points into each PC's next single tech (BattleSys_SpendTechPoints, BattleSys_TryNextTech), learning it when its cost is covered (BattleSys_LearnSingleTech); a tech whose record has bit 7 pays nothing until the character's bit in Battle_Unk7F01E0 is set ("not open to it yet; probably magic"). The points are also added to the PC's .TechPtTotal. Then BattleSys_BuildComboMasks forms the party's pairs and trio, and BattleSys_LearnComboTechs sets the double and triple techs whose members have each learned enough single techs.

Quirks the headers keep:

  • BattleSys_SpendTechPoints takes the award (or the last leftover) off the next tech's need a second time, so tech points are counted twice "as the code reads"; NEXT.md marks it as worth a check in an emulator.
  • A character not in the battle gains at most one level per battle, and the experience past that level is not carried into .ExpNeed.
  • The messages for new double and triple techs go to the last PC slot with a character, not to each member.
  • The 9,999,999 caps of .Exp and .TechPtTotal do not catch every overflow.

docs.title: Battler upkeep
docs.text: $C1:B093–$C1:B487: the low-HP bit (HP at most an eighth of the maximum), which turn lists a battler takes part in from its status bits, the KO check with a one-time revive (BattleSys_UpdateKo), and the copies back to the field at the end (FieldBtlObj flags, the character records). The turn helpers ($C1:B4E9–$C1:B80C) refund items, build the PCs' command groups from their partner bytes, and handle a battle with fixed commands (Battle_Unk2989 bit 5, "a demo, probably" in NEXT.md).

docs.title: Bank $FD helpers
docs.text: BattleFD_* ($FD:A982–$FD:B956, 40 routines) are the battle's long callees: clearing work RAM, restoring enemies, the end messages and rewards (BattleFD_AddEnemyRewards, BattleFD_AddItemEntry), the battlers' records, the enemies' stats, the turn-list timers and the first ATB values. They run in the battle's state and use bank $C1's direct-page scratch and math cells. Five JSR/RTL veneers at $C1:FDBF–$C1:FDD2 (Battle_Mul16Long, BankC1_AddItemLong, BattleSys_RunPcAttackLong, Battle_RandRangeLong, BattleSys_RefundItemLong) let them call back into bank $C1. Most keep Unk names because verified code calls them by name; NEXT.md lists better names for when those callers are reviewed again.

docs.title: Shared services and helpers
docs.text:
• Inventory and gold services for the field: BankC1_Entry8003 ($C1:8003) leads to BankC1_RunService ($C1:CFC2) and BankC1_ServiceTable ($C1:D126): 0 find an item, 1 add one, 2 remove one, 3 test the 24-bit gold against an amount, 4 add gold, 5 take gold off when there is that much. The event opcodes $C7, $C9–$CE use them (see Field event scripts).
  • The service dispatcher at $C1:0045 (table at $C1:0051, reached only by same-bank JSR): 1 enqueue a ready battler, 2 remove one, 3 two frames of upkeep, 4 play an action, 5 position queries (BattlePos_Query), 7 target area query, 8 victory pose, 9 defeat pose; service 0 ends in Battle_StartPose, service 6 is not analysed.
  • Frame wait: BattleSys_PumpFrames ($C1:007E), a frame wait by inference (see Frame cycle and NMI).
  • Maths: Battle_Mul8, Battle_Mul8x16 and Battle_Divide on the hardware maths unit ($C1:0089–$C1:010C), the overlapping shift tails ($C1:010D–$C1:011E), the shift-and-add Battle_Mul16 and Battle_Div32 ($C1:C90B–$C1:C95B), and Battle_RandRange ($C1:AF22), a random number in a range from RandomTableFD, and Battle_RandRangeAlt ($C1:AF79), the same with its own index into the table.
  • Geometry: Battle_SinLookup and Battle_CalcAngle ($C1:01F9–$C1:0298, 256 steps per turn); battler boxes and their collision tests ($C1:283D–$C1:2985); the position queries of service 5 ($C1:2986–$C1:2D9E: nearest or farthest PC or enemy, distance checks, a path check, screen-half tests).

docs.title: Battle menu
docs.text:
The battle command menu in bank $C1 ($C1:0785–$C1:1C49, plus BattleMenu_BuildTargetList at $C1:1F79): the per-PC command windows, the tech and item lists, the input handlers for each window, the queue of PCs waiting for a command, and the cursor sprites. It runs with M=1, X=0, DP=0 and DB=$7E, like the rest of the battle.

See also: Battle targeting, Status bar & text, Battle engine.

docs.title: The rebuild chain
docs.text:
The menu is not redrawn every frame: it rebuilds only on frames where !BattleMenu_Dirty is set. Three routines gate it the same way: BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL ($C1:10E3, the JSL form), BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyAndTick ($C1:10FA, which also runs a per-frame service tick and is called after each frame wait of an action) and BattleSys_UpkeepTwoFrames (service 3). Each one clears the flag and runs the chain:

  1. BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler: take the next PC off the ready queue;
  2. BattleMenu_UpdateWindows ($C1:0C2D): window upkeep by submenu: the main command window (BattleMenu_UpdateMainWindow), the tech window (BattleMenu_UpdateTechWindow, with the MP check of each visible tech in BattleMenu_UpdateTechMpAvail), or the item window;
  3. BattleMenu_ProcessInput ($C1:1153): the command window's input;
  4. BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay ($C1:17DD, 828 bytes): draw whichever cursor belongs on screen now: none, the target cursor(s), the tech-list cursor (a 2–3 sprite cluster over the partners for a double or triple tech) or the item-list cursor and scroll arrows.

docs.title: The ready queue
docs.text: Services 1 and 2 of the battle's service dispatcher manage the PCs waiting for a command: BattleMenu_EnqueueReadyBattler ($C1:1B19) marks the PC's command record "waiting for a command", appends it to !BattleMenu_ReadyQueue and plays sound $42 (inferred: the "turn ready" cue); BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady ($C1:1BAA) is its inverse. BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler pops the head (up to 3 deep) into the roster of PCs shown in the menu. BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev / Next switch between the roster's PCs.

docs.title: Windows and lists
docs.text:
• Command window: BattleMenu_DrawCommandList and BattleMenu_DrawCommandWindowFrames ($C1:0785–$C1:095C) draw each roster PC's commands; BattleMenu_LoadCommandWindowMap copies the window map from ROM. BattleMenu_CursorUp / Down move between rows; BattleMenu_ConfirmCommand dispatches row 0 (attack, BattleMenu_ChooseAttack), row 1 (tech, BattleMenu_OpenTechList) and row 2 (item, BattleMenu_OpenItemList).
  • Tech list (submenu 1): BattleMenu_RenderTechListRows / RenderTechRow copy tech names from the tables in bank $CC; BattleMenu_TechListInput ($C1:1320) with TechListPrev / Next, TechConfirm and TechListCancel.
  • Item list (submenu 2): BattleMenu_RenderItemListRows / RenderItemRow; BattleMenu_ItemListInput ($C1:143D) with cursor, page and scroll handlers, ItemConfirm and ItemListCancel.

docs.title: Choosing a target and committing
docs.text:
Confirming an attack, tech or item builds the target list (BattleMenu_BuildTargetList, see Battle targeting) and switches to target selection, whose input is BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput ($C1:1561; BattleMenu_TargetNext / Prev cycle the cursor). Confirming a target runs BattleMenu_CommitAction ($C1:161A): it fills the PC's BattleCmd record (kind $80 attack, $20 tech, $40 item; the partners; the action id; the first selected target), consumes the partners of a double or triple tech (BattleMenu_ConsumePartnerSlot) so they do not act too, decrements the item's quantity, appends the PC to !Battle_CmdQueue and shows the next roster entry. The battle's turn handler later runs the command (see Battle engine).

docs.title: Status bar & text
docs.text:
The battle's status bar and the number and text formatting it uses, in bank $C1 ($C1:011F–$C1:01F8, $C1:0299–$C1:095C, $C1:104E). The status bar is built as a tilemap in WRAM (BattleUI_StatusTile, $7E:0CC0, 192 entries) with each PC's name, HP, MP and, in two of its three layouts, the ATB gauge; the enemies' names share it.

See also: Battle menu, Battle engine.

docs.title: The status bar
docs.text:
BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame ($C1:0299, falling into BattleUI_DrawPcNamePanel and BattleUI_NextNamePanel, which run to $C1:05A6) rebuilds the whole map:

  1. clear it;
  2. write the "HP"/"MP" headers where the layout (!BattleUI_GaugeLayout) puts them: layout 0 is name, HP/MaxHP, MP; layout 1 is HP, MP, name, ATB gauge; layout 2 is name, HP, MP, ATB gauge;
  3. for each present PC: its 10 name tiles (5 on the line, 5 on the row above), the HP digits (in palette 3 when HP is 0, or at most an eighth of the maximum while a flag is set), and the MaxHP digits or the gauge with its end caps;
  4. the enemy-name lines (11 tiles on each of two rows);
  5. while PCs wait for a command, the command windows (or, while choosing a target from a submenu, the highlight of the targeted PC's name, BattleUI_HighlightPcName).

The per-frame peer is BattleUI_UpdateNextPcPanel ($C1:05A7): it refreshes one PC's HP and MP digits per call, round robin, then redraws every present PC's ATB gauge (BattleUI_DrawAtbGauges, layouts 1 and 2). BattleMenu_UpdateMainWindow calls the full rebuild when the shown PC changes and this one otherwise.

BattleUI_DrawSlotGaugeBar ($C1:06F0) draws a PC's 4-tile ATB gauge: the filled part is AtbCur × 256 / AtbMax scaled to 32 units, and the tiles drawn track the part still to fill, in palette 3 while AtbCur is non-zero. What the tiles look like depends on the graphics, which were not checked.

docs.title: Numbers and text
docs.text:
Routine Address Does BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits $C1:011F A value 0–999 into three digit tiles (thousands blank) BattleMsg_FormatTwoDigits $C1:0174 Tens and ones only BattleMsg_BlankLeadingZeros $C1:104E Leading-zero suppression for the digits BattleMsg_ReencodeTextBuffer $C1:01A9 Re-encode 16 text bytes into a row of tiles and a row of marks above them (probably the dakuten and handakuten of the Japanese text code, a leftover) BattleMsg_FormatNumber4Digits $CF:FDAD A four-digit, long-call version of the formatter, in bank $CF

The formatters count digits with subtract-and-count loops on a 16-bit accumulator, so their SBC/ADC immediates carry an explicit .w (asar does not track the M flag).

docs.title: Battle targeting
docs.text:
Choosing who an action hits ($C1:1FDD–$C1:283C): the table of target modes and their handlers, the four area shapes, and the candidate-list helpers. The menu side that drives it (BattleMenu_BuildTargetList, the target-select input and the commit) is on the Battle menu page; the position queries of service 5 are on Battle engine.

See also: Battle menu, Battle actions.

docs.title: Target modes
docs.text:
BattleMenu_BuildTargetList ($C1:1F79) records the caster, blanks the candidate and selection lists (!BattleTgt_Candidates, !BattleTgt_Selected, battler slots 0–2 for the PCs and 3–10 for the enemies), and runs the handler for !BattleTgt_Mode & $7F (clamped to $20) from BattleTgt_ModeTable ($C1:1FF8, 33 words). Each handler fills the candidates, seeds the selection from the cursor, and says whether the player may move the cursor (!BattleTgt_CanCycle) or the action hits the whole list (!BattleTgt_TargetAll = $80). An empty selection means "no valid target".

Modes Handler Targets others BattleTgt_SingleAlly One PC, cursor may cycle (the default) $01, $04 BattleTgt_AllAllies All PCs $02 BattleTgt_Self The caster $03 BattleTgt_SingleKoAlly One PC whose status bit 7 is set (by context, a KO'd ally) $05, $06 BattleTgt_PcByCharId5 / 4 The party member with a given character id $07 BattleTgt_SingleEnemy One enemy, cursor may cycle $08, $0A BattleTgt_AllEnemies All enemies $09 BattleTgt_Everyone Everyone $0B–$0D BattleTgt_EnemyLineFrom* Enemies on a line from a PC toward a chosen enemy $0F, $11–$14, $18, $1A, $1B radius, row and triangle handlers Enemies inside a circle, a row band, or the triangle of the three PCs

docs.title: Area shapes
docs.text:
The area modes pick an anchor (the caster, a chosen enemy, or a particular party member), fill the area parameter block (!BattleTgt_AreaCentre, AreaAim, AreaSize, AreaVariant, AreaSide), run one geometry routine that writes the battlers it hits into the candidates, and select the whole list:

Routine Address Shape BattleTgt_AreaRow $C1:2332 A band of ±$20 around the anchor's screen Y BattleTgt_AreaPartyTriangle $C1:23A4 Inside the triangle whose corners are the three PCs BattleTgt_AreaLine $C1:25A3 Along the line from a source toward the aimed-at battler BattleTgt_AreaCircle $C1:2701 Within a radius of the centre battler

Some handlers look for a specific party member: BattleTgt_EnemyLineFromChar3 and BattleTgt_Char3Radius use the member with character id 3 (!Pc_CharRobo, inferred: Robo), and BattleTgt_Char6Radius the member with id 6; they return early when no PC has that id. The enemy-anchored modes let the D-pad move the aim, with a sound on each step.

Service 7 (BattleTgt_RunAreaQuery, $C1:1FDD) runs one of the same geometry routines by !BattleTgt_AreaType through BattleTgt_AreaTable (7 entries). Its header reads it as "presumably" how code outside the menu (enemy scripts, scripted attacks) asks which battlers an area hits.

docs.title: Boot
docs.text:
Power-on and reset, from the vectors at the top of bank $C0 (seen by the CPU as bank $00) to the start of the game loop. All of it is matched: the reset code, the interrupt stubs and vectors, the ROM header, MainInit in bank $FD, and the cold init at the start of GameLoop.

See also: Frame cycle and NMI, ROM Map, Architecture.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
The vector table RomVectors ($00:FFE0–$FFFF) uses only four entries; every other slot is $FFFF:

Vector Address Target Native BRK $FFE6 BRK_Handler ($00:FF18) Native NMI $FFEA NMI_Stub ($00:FF10) Native IRQ $FFEE IRQ_Stub ($00:FF14) Emulation COP $FFF4 BRK_Handler Emulation RESET $FFFC Reset ($00:FF00)

The emulation-mode NMI is unused: the NMI is off after reset during the three instructions Reset runs in emulation mode.

  • Reset ($00:FF00): SEI, CLC, XCE (native mode), JML MainInit. The SEI is for the soft resets, which arrive in native mode: Menu_PollPad ($C2:8523) jumps here when L+R+Select+Start are held, and two unmatched sites in banks $C3 and $CF do too.
  • NMI_Stub / IRQ_Stub: the native vectors can only point into bank $00, so these jump on through 4-byte trampolines in WRAM ($7E:0500, $7E:0504) that the game rewrites as it changes mode.
  • BRK_Handler: a crash trap; it reads a fixed address forever and never returns (the read is what a bus trace or debugger would see, inferred).

The cartridge header ($00:FFB0–$FFDF, RomExtHeader to RomChecksum) reads: maker "C3", game code "ACTE", title "CHRONO TRIGGER", HiROM + FastROM ($31), ROM + RAM + battery, 4 MB of ROM, 8 KB of save RAM, North America, version 1.0.

docs.title: MainInit
docs.text:
MainInit ($FD:C000, 215 bytes) puts the CPU and PPU into a known state in five steps. Every register write goes through a relocated direct page, so each store is two bytes:

  1. CPU mode, stack (S = $06FF), DB = $00, DP = $4200 ($FD:C000–$C013);
  2. the CPU I/O registers through DP = $4200 ($FD:C014–$C035);
  3. DP = $2100, the screen into forced blank ($FD:C036–$C041);
  4. the PPU registers through DP = $2100 ($FD:C042–$C0D2); most are zeroed;
  5. JML GameLoop ($FD:C0D3).

It leaves with interrupts, NMI, DMA and HDMA off. It is also reached by JML MainInit at $C0:418D, in Evt_OpFF96_Reset (event opcode $FF $96), after InitHW: the game restarts from its cold start. Ppu_SetBgLayout ($FD:C0D7), right after it, sets a fixed background layout the same way.

docs.title: GameLoop's cold init
docs.text:
GameLoop ($C0:000E) installs the interrupt trampolines (InstallNMI: JML NmiHandler into $7E:0500; InstallIRQ: JML IrqHandler into $7E:0504), sets DP = $0100, runs InitHW (interrupts off, forced blank, NMI, DMA and HDMA off, DB = $00), and clears WRAM with ClearRAMDMA in three blocks ($7E:0000–04FF, $7E:0700–FFFF, $7F:5080–A0FF), leaving the trampolines and the stack alone. ClearRAMDMA ($C0:2DF1) fills with DMA channel 7 from the PPU's Mode 7 multiply result (MPYL), which reads 0 because both operands are 0. Then it starts the sound driver (JSL Audio_DriverInit, bank $C7) and sends bank $C2 its start-up command (JSL BankC2_Entry8004), and falls into GameLoop_Main.

GameLoop is reached a second time by BRL from Scene_Unk0283 (probably the game-over path). The review of MainInit noted that its name is probably wrong, since it starts with an init sequence rather than a loop.

docs.title: Engine core
docs.text:
Bank $C0's field engine: the game loop and its per-frame calls, location loading, the map (collision, tile effects, scrolling and redraws), the field's scene changes and its hand-off to the battle and to bank $C2, window effects, the staff credits, and the object motion code. Three parts have pages of their own: Frame cycle and NMI, Field event scripts and Sprites & objects.

The field code runs with DP=$0100 (the field page, names in asm/include/ram_engine.inc) and DB=$00; the map code switches to DP=$1D00 (!DP_Map). The function table at the bottom of this page lists every routine in the "Engine" group, which also takes in the matched code of banks $C2 and $FD that has no group of its own; "Engine (unnamed)" holds the two routines still labelled Sub_: Sub_1ADF (purpose unknown) and Sub_C07F9A (no reader of its results traced).

See also: Architecture, Boot, Sprite Init Explainer, ROM Map.

docs.title: The game loop
docs.text:
GameLoop_LoadField ($C0:007D) loads a location and falls into GameLoop_FrameBody ($C0:0097), which runs, every frame: Field_PauseAndMenuInput, Field_SceneChangeTick, Field_FrameUpdate, Field_ActionButton, Field_Unk1F87 (the message window's step; see Field event scripts), Field_EventHookDispatch, Field_ServiceUnk54, Field_EndOfFrame and Field_WaitFrame. See Architecture for the order and Frame cycle and NMI for the end of the frame.

  • Field_PauseAndMenuInput ($C0:18D9): Start pauses (the brightness halves until Start is pressed again); the menu button fades out, saves the field and calls bank $C2's menu entry ("very likely the main menu", per its header).
  • Field_FrameUpdate ($C0:881E): with DP=$1D00, the D-pad (Field_DpadDispatch and its 16-entry table), the leader's collision (Map_Unk8A6D, probably), the step limits and the layer scroll (Map_Unk91AC, Map_Unk93E1).
  • Field_ActionButton ($C0:1AAC): on the action button, looks for an object in front of the leader (Field_FindObjInFront) and starts its function 1, then checks the tile in front for treasure (Field_CheckTileInFront).

docs.title: Loading a location
docs.text:
LoadLocation ($C0:00F4) runs ten steps and two bank-$FD vectors:

Step Does LocLoad_Unk092B Find the location's record (LocRom) from Loc_Id LocLoad_AudioSetup The sound step LocLoad_Unk0960 Layers 1 and 2 graphics LocLoad_Unk6DCF Layer 3 graphics (or none) LocLoad_Unk7084 The location's palette rows LocLoad_ClearPage1D00 Zero the map page LocLoad_UnkA33B Map properties: layer sizes and screen settings, then the wrap masks and limits, the tile planes and the exit tiles LocLoad_Unk09DD, LocLoad_Unk0A14 The layer 1/2 and layer 3 metatile tables LocLoad_Unk56D4 Unpack and check the event data FdVec_FFFA, FdVec_FFF4 Location animation set-up (FieldFD_LoadAnimSetA/B): records at $05B0 and $0520, probably the tile and palette animations

Then Scene_PostLoadInit ($C0:56A6) resets the object tables and runs every object's init script, and Scene_SettleFrames runs Scene_ReloadStep ($C0:286C: draw the map with LocLoad_DrawMap, reset the objects, the uploads and palettes, NMI back on) and fades in. Most steps keep Unk names because verified callers use them; NEXT.md lists the better names waiting for those callers' next review.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
The map is kept in WRAM as metatiles; the map code runs with DP=$1D00.

  • Collision and tile effects ($C0:8A6D–$C0:9174, $C0:9923–$C0:9DC2): Map_Unk8A6D tests the frame's step against the leader's box with probes for other objects (Map_ProbeHitsObj) and for the map tile under a point (Map_ProbeTileAttrs, Map_ProbeTileLevel, Map_ProbeLevelBlocked), and slides along walls. Map_StepTileEffects commits a kept step: an exit tile requests a warp (from the ExitRom records in bank $E5, "inferred: an exit tile"), a tile with attribute bit 4 requests a tile animation, and the tile's level and push are applied. Map_InitEntryTile is its sibling at load time.
  • Scrolling ($C0:91AC–$C0:9922): Map_Unk91AC adds up the frame's scroll amounts for three sets of layer scroll words in 1/16 pixel (with a scroll-to target and a screen shake) and splits out whole pixels; Map_Unk93E1 steps the words a pixel at a time and notes each 8-pixel boundary crossed. The 16 edge builders Map_BuildRow* / Map_BuildCol* ($C0:8243–$C0:8444) build the new row or column, and the NMI uploads it (Map_UploadRowYInc1 …).
  • Redraws ($C0:75E9–$C0:8242): whole-layer redraws into the $7E:C800 buffer (Field_BuildC800Mode1/2/4), the row and column writers, and the VRAM uploads (Map_UploadBuf*), driven by DefaultHandler's redraw request and Field_Unk885A.
  • Tile animations: the five handlers ModeE6_Handler … ModeFC_Handler ($C0:0D78–$C0:16DB) advance a map tile's state byte and queue the VRAM addresses of its 8×8 tiles for doors and switches that open over a few frames (see Architecture). The field IRQ writes the new tilemap words (see Frame cycle and NMI). TileAnimList (16 words at $7F:1CC8, $C0:28AA–$C0:29F6) remembers the tiles whose animation ran at this location, so that a reload (Scene_ReloadStep) puts their final states back into Map_TileProps before the map is drawn.

docs.title: Scene changes, fades and hand-offs
docs.text:
Field_SceneChangeTick ($C0:0C76) and DefaultHandler ($C0:16DC) act on the scene request bits: warp, bank-$C2 call, tile animation, single tile step, map redraw and battle (see Architecture). The fades are Fade_StepBrightness and Fade_StepFixedColor ($C0:1F24, $C0:1F5A).

  • Bank $C2 round trips: Field_SaveState / Field_RestoreState ($C0:011B, $C0:01A5) save and rebuild the field around a call to BankC2_Entry8000, with Field_StashSaveBlock / Field_RestoreSaveBlock copying the $14E0-byte save block to $7F:2000 and back.
  • Battle hand-off ($C0:0283–$C0:0904): before a battle Field_Unk038F fills the hand-off block (FieldBtlPc, FieldBtlObj, FieldBtlPpu at $7E:29B0–$2C7B) with the party's positions, the objects and the PPU state; afterwards Scene_Unk0283 reads FieldBtl_Result and rebuilds in place (FieldBtl_Restore), reloads the location, or restarts the game (probably the game-over path).

docs.title: Services for other banks
docs.text:
ReentryVectors entries 1–4 ($C0:0002–$C0:000B) are JSL targets for code in other banks (the calling sites are in banks $CD and $D1, not matched):

  • ScrollStepAccum ($C0:2C41): steps the scroll positions of layers 2 and 3 by signed per-frame speeds in 1/16 pixel and stores them into the battle hand-off's FieldBtlPpu.Scroll2 words; its header suggests the name LayerDrift_Step, "probably the battle backgrounds' drift". DefaultHandler calls it too.
  • Field_RefreshHdmaLong ($C0:0AFF, formerly the stub AudioDrvSync; it touches no sound): runs EngFD_UnkC2C1 twice, so both of its handler tables run once, sets up the HDMA channels and returns the HDMA channel mask.
  • MusicCueDispatch ($C0:1BAB): "before a battle, probably". With FieldBtl_EvtKeepMusic clear it sends sound command $14 with a track ($45 at load, "the battle music, probably"); with it set, command $70.
  • AudioFadeDispatch ($C0:1BE6): "after a battle, probably", by FieldBtl_Result. Result 1 ("the party lost, probably") sends command $14 with song $26; otherwise, unless FieldBtl_EvtKeepMusic is set, it sends command $11 with Menu_Config1E (where Evt_OpEA_PlayMusic keeps the track it starts). It restores DB and D in the wrong order, which is harmless only when the caller has D = 0 and DB = 0; kept as found.

docs.title: Window effects and credits
docs.text:
• Field_EventHookDispatch ($C0:21E1) runs one of 16 hooks from Field_EventHookTable: growing and shrinking window shapes on the BG or colour windows, a shape from four moving points, fixed shapes, a pulsing shape that runs its own frames, and a hook that leaves the field for good (Field_HookLeaveToBankC3).
  • Field_ServiceUnk54 ($C0:274D) builds the staff credits a line at a time from the text at $FD:A000 (the NMI sends each line with Credits_UploadLine), and passes map redraw requests on to the NMI.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text: The per-frame object pass Vblank_UnkA810 ($C0:A810) moves every object (Obj_MoveStep, Obj_MoveStepFree), tests it against a window a little larger than the view (Obj_UpdateInView), ticks its animation and puts it in the draw bucket for its screen position. Obj_CalcDirection, Obj_SetVelocity and Obj_SetVelocityChecked ($C0:ABA2–$C0:AF2F) set up moves for the event opcodes. The party members' objects step through Evt_OpB0_PartyControl's callees ($C0:9E29–$C0:A33A): the leader's step (Party_Unk9E29) logs each frame it moves in a 128-entry ring in bank $7F, and members 2 and 3 (Party_UnkA26B, Party_UnkA2CE) replay it $18 entries behind the one ahead ($10 when the leader stands), so they walk the leader's path. Each picks its facing and animation row (walk, run, stand or idle) from the step through Party_AnimTable ($C0:9FF7, 65 words). Positions are in 1/16 pixel; the high byte is the 16-pixel map tile. The tile-slot and palette-slot allocators (Obj_TileSlot*, Obj_PalSlot*, $C0:6F9A–$C0:7083, $C0:7170–$C0:7398) give objects VRAM and palette space by kind. See Sprites & objects for drawing.

docs.title: Bank $FD field code
docs.text: The field HDMA set-up (EngFD_UnkC124, Hdma_InitChannelsFD, EngFD_UnkC2C1 with its two handler tables, $FD:C124–$FD:C2EA, and EngFD_UnkD52D), and the location animation set-up (FieldFD_LoadAnimSetA / B and the vectors FdVec_FFF4 / FFF7 / FFFA).

docs.title: What is not matched yet
docs.text:
Bank $C0 is fully matched. Its last code is the message choice cursor that the field IRQ draws (Irq_DrawChoiceCursor, $C0:F05E; see Frame cycle and NMI), and after that the bank holds only data (see the ROM Map). From NEXT.md, what is left of the field code is in bank $FD: the IRQ's other phase FdVec_FFFD, the HDMA builders behind EngFD_UnkC2C1's tables, and EngFD_UnkE39C (FdVec_FFF7's target).

docs.title: Field event scripts
docs.text:
Every object on a field location (people, doors, the party members themselves) is driven by a byte-code script in the location's event data. The interpreter, the opcode table (Evt_OpcodeTable, $C0:5D6E, 256 words) and every opcode handler are in bank $C0 and matched; what is left is outside the interpreter (see What is not matched yet).

See also: Frame cycle and NMI, Engine core, Sprites & objects.

docs.title: Objects, functions and levels
docs.text:
LocLoad_Unk56D4 ($C0:56D4), the last location-load step, unpacks the event data; LocLoad_CheckEvtData checks it and stops the game on a colour (Sys_HaltWithColor) if it is bad. The data starts with a function table: 16 function offsets per object (32 bytes per object at Evt_Data + slot × 16, the slot being the object number × 2).

Evt_InitObjects ($C0:5709) resets the per-object tables for the location's Evt_ObjCount objects and runs each object's function 0 (its init function) up to opcode $00. Evt_RunObjInit ($C0:597D) does the same for one object; Party_ReinitIfChanged uses it for the character objects after a bank-$C2 round trip.

Each object runs at a level (Obj_Unk1C00), 7 after its init function. The function-call banner reads lower levels as more urgent, "probably": a call only interrupts an object running at a higher level. A call saves the interrupted script position in a per-level table (ObjX_Unk7F0580), and Evt_Op00_Return ($C0:5F74) resumes the first saved position above the level that ends. The action button (Field_ActionButton → Evt_StartTargetFunc1) starts function 1 of the object found in front of the leader; Evt_StartTargetFunc2 is the touch counterpart (function 2).

docs.title: The scheduler
docs.text:
Scripts run from Field_EndOfFrame, once per frame, in two steps ($C0:59D9–$C0:5AC4):

  1. Vblank_Unk59D9 counts down every object's script timer (Obj_Unk1001, reloaded from Obj_Unk1000, 4 at load) and queues the objects whose timer ran out (kind-0 objects at the head of the list, others at the tail).
  2. Vblank_ReadScanlineCounters runs the queued objects while the frame still has time: before each object it reads the PPU's V counter and stops once it is at ObjQ_Unk69 ($48 from Scene_PostLoadInit) or more but below line 240.
  3. Evt_RunObjScriptSteps ($C0:5A93) runs one object: up to Field_Unk68 opcodes (5 from load) through Evt_OpcodeTable.

Every handler is entered with Y = its opcode's offset in the event data and returns X = where the script goes on, with C=1 to run the next opcode in this run or C=0 to stop the object until its next run. A handler that returns its own position with C=0 runs again next time: that is how waits and moves in progress work. The two scheduler routines keep their Vblank_ names because verified callers use them; their headers suggest Obj_QueueScripts / Obj_RunQueuedScripts.

docs.title: The opcodes
docs.text:
Evt_OpcodeTable ($C0:5D6E–$C0:5F6D) holds one bank-$C0 handler address per opcode. Four places read it with JSR (Evt_OpcodeTable,X): Evt_InitObjects, Evt_RunObj0Func1, Evt_RunObjInit and Evt_RunObjScriptSteps. Its first two bytes are also read by the 32-byte copies of LocLoad_InitUnk7F3700 (see Party walks).
